#9812. Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:

LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:

The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders:

Each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:

For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:

#9810. Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:

The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

What's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

#9808. Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

This entry was posted on Wednesday 4th of November 2026 11:36 PM

#9807. Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:

Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

#9806. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?

SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

AI finally makes it possible to automate the coordination layer that's been killing their time. Two years ago the AI wasn't good enough. Two years from now every big player will have copied it. Now is the window.

It's just me right now, and that's actually the point. I'm not a developer who discovered influencer marketing. I'm an influencer marketer who learned to build. I've lived inside this problem for 6 years across 1,000+ campaigns and over $5M in spend. I know exactly what breaks, when it breaks, and why. Nobody is closer to this customer than I am because I am the customer.

Honestly? Still managing influencer campaigns and complaining about the lack of good tools. Brief exists because I got tired of waiting for someone else to build it.

Right now, paying customers and retention. I care about teams that come back every month because Brief is how they run their business.

Brief is the AI PM and CRM for influencer marketing teams. It manages campaigns from brief to invoice automatically, it simplifies creator partnerships and content approvals.

#9804. Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

Today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026

The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge

The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

#9803. Self-Hosted Indian Language STT Server – VEXYL-STT Open Source

Posted on Nov 8 • Originally published at vexyl.ai • AI-assisted

If you’ve ever tried to add self-hosted Indian language speech to text to a production system, you know the problem. Cloud STT APIs either don’t support Indian languages well, charge per-minute fees that kill your margins, or send audio to servers in the US — which is a non-starter for healthcare and government use cases. We built VEXYL-STT to fix this, and today we’re releasing it as open source.

VEXYL-STT is a free, self-hosted speech-to-text server wrapping AI4Bharat’s IndicConformer 600M multilingual model. It supports 14 Indian languages, runs on CPU (no GPU required for typical workloads), and exposes both a WebSocket streaming API and a REST batch API on a single port. Apache 2.0 licensed. No API keys. No per-minute billing. Your audio never leaves your server.

VEXYL-STT started as an internal component of the VEXYL AI Voice Gateway — our enterprise platform that bridges Asterisk/FreePBX telephony infrastructure with modern AI services. We needed a self-hosted STT option for deployments where cloud APIs are not viable: hospitals with patient audio data, government agencies with data sovereignty requirements, and enterprises that simply can’t afford ₹1–3 per minute of STT billing at scale.

We chose AI4Bharat’s IndicConformer 600M multilingual model as the backbone because, frankly, nothing else comes close for Indian languages. It’s the most capable open-source Indian ASR model available, trained on thousands of hours of Indic language audio across 22 official languages. We extracted the STT component, wrapped it in a production-ready server, and are now releasing it so the community can use it independently.

The current release supports 14 Indian languages out of the box:

Switch between languages at the session level — no server restart needed. Just pass the language code in your WebSocket start message or batch API request. If you pass an unknown code, it defaults to Malayalam (ml).

VEXYL-STT runs two modes on a single port — you don’t need to run separate services for streaming vs. batch use cases.

Connect over WebSocket, send raw 16kHz 16-bit mono PCM audio as binary frames, and receive JSON transcripts in real time. The server uses energy-based VAD to detect speech boundaries and fires a final message when an utterance completes. This is the right mode for telephony integrations, browser mic capture, and any scenario where you’re streaming live audio.

For file-based transcription or systems with their own VAD (including our own VEXYL Voice Gateway which uses Silero VAD v5), the batch API accepts WAV, MP3, FLAC, OGG, and M4A files up to 25MB / 5 minutes. Submit a file, poll for status, retrieve the transcript. Supported formats cover almost everything you’ll encounter in the field.

The quickest path is the automated setup script. You’ll need Python 3.10+, a HuggingFace account with access approved for the gated IndicConformer model, and about 3GB of free disk space for the model weights.

For Docker deployments, pass your HuggingFace token as a build arg and the model gets baked into the image:

One thing worth knowing before you start: the HuggingFace gated model approval is required. If you hit a 401 or 403, run huggingface-cli whoami and verify your token has read access and that your access request has been approved. This catches most people out.

I’ll be direct: if you’re doing low-volume transcription with no data sovereignty concerns, Sarvam AI’s API is excellent and I’d use it. But if you’re running at scale, building in healthcare, or deploying for government — the economics and compliance picture shifts dramatically in favour of self-hosting.

The latency numbers above are from our production deployment at a tertiary care hospital in Kerala processing Malayalam patient interactions. On the same VPS, local WebSocket transcription consistently returns under 350ms. Cloud providers add network round-trip time on top of model inference — which matters a lot when you’re building a real-time voice assistant.

The IndicConformer model supports both CTC and RNNT decoding. VEXYL-STT defaults to CTC because it’s faster — typically 30–50% lower latency on CPU. RNNT is more accurate, especially for longer utterances and noisy telephony audio, but adds latency.

My recommendation: start with CTC (VEXYL_STT_DECODE=ctc), measure your accuracy on real audio, and switch to RNNT (VEXYL_STT_DECODE=rnnt) if accuracy is the limiting factor rather than latency. For most patient interaction use cases we’ve tested, CTC accuracy is sufficient and the latency advantage is worth it.

A few things we learned running this in production that aren’t obvious from the docs:

VEXYL-STT is actively maintained and we welcome contributions — new language support, performance improvements, integration examples, and documentation. Star the repo if it’s useful, open an issue if you find a bug, and submit a PR if you’ve built something on top of it.

If you’re looking to go further — full telephony AI with Asterisk, multi-language IVR, voice bots for healthcare or enterprise — that’s what the VEXYL AI Voice Gateway is built for. It’s a self-hosted platform where you bring your own provider keys, with support for Indian languages over PSTN and SIP.

Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

Sellfy has its benefits and downsides, but fortunately, the pros outweigh the cons.

#9801. Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

#9800. What Fact-Checking My Own Claude Code Guide Taught Me About Verifiable AI

Copy trader and developer. I publish my real results, losses included, and the tools I use to pick traders. Open source at github.com/benryandev

Copy trader and developer. I publish my real results, losses included, and the tools I use to pick traders. Open source at github.com/benryandev

Copy trader and developer. I publish my real results, losses included, and the tools I use to pick traders. Open source at github.com/benryandev

Most talk about verifiable AI is about the model: proofs of inference, attested hardware, reproducible weights. That matters. But most of the AI output people act on every day isn't a model call they could audit. It's a claim: in a doc, a README, an answer, a config someone copied.

I write about Claude Code. In February, I published a long guide to building with it, plus a companion GitHub repo of the configs I actually use. The repo is the part a reader can copy straight into their own setup, which turns out to matter. As Veera Ravindra Divi put it here on HackerNoon, Claude Code doesn't ship production code: your config does. A wrong config does more damage than a wrong sentence.

Since then I've re-checked every claim in it twice, once in August against Claude Code v2.1.234 and again this month against v2.1.311, the second time with four Claude Code agents working in parallel. I expected stale facts. What I didn't expect was ten claims that were wrong on the day I wrote them. One of them was a correction from the August pass.

This month, the agents did most of the checking. Some of their findings looked like errors until I traced the source, and some of my old claims looked fine until I did the same. Either way, what mattered was whether a verdict could be checked by someone other than whoever produced it.

A verified claim needs four things. I learned each one by watching a check fail without it.

A checker citing the article it's checking

None of these is about the model. You can run the best model available and still get output you can't verify. You can also run a cheaper one and get output anyone can audit, if the process makes it leave a trail.

Every one of these is fluent, specific, and plausible. That is the kind of claim language models produce easily, and agents repeat confidently. It is also the kind a reader can't check without a source.

Look at numbers 5, 7 and 8. A version number, a percentage, and a line count. Each one survived review because it was specific.

"Compaction triggers at about 95%" sounds like someone measured it. "Before v2.1.179" sounds like someone read the changelog. Nobody had. The precision did the persuading, and the precision was invented.

My rule now: every number gets a source next to it, or it gets rewritten as a range or removed. When the first correction pass suggested "fixed around v2.1.63" for a GitHub issue, there was no changelog entry behind it. That number came out too. The guide now says the behaviour is no longer reproducible and tells readers to check it themselves with /context.

Checking against official documentation sounds definitive until two official sources disagree.

In August, Claude Code's subagents page still listed a 200-subagent-per-session cap. The changelog said it was removed in v2.1.224. The docs hadn't caught up.

In October, Anthropic's API models page listed Sonnet 5.5's default effort as high. Claude Code's model configuration page says the 5.5 models default to medium. Both are right: one describes the API, the other describes Claude Code. An agent that reads only one of them will "correct" a true claim into a false one.

So provenance has to include which system and which version a source describes. For anything version-specific, I treat the changelog as the primary source. When sources disagree, the verdict says which surface each one describes rather than quietly picking one.

The worst error in the February guide isn't on the list above. Nothing I wrote was false; I left something out.

Agent Teams is experimental and disabled by default. It needs CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1. I never mentioned it, because the flag had sat in my own settings.json so long I'd stopped seeing it. Every Agent Teams pattern in the guide worked on my machine and did nothing on yours.

Reading docs can't catch that. The docs are right, and the claim is right. What's missing is the environment. The only check that works is re-running the instructions somewhere that isn't your machine.

The same applies to the repo's example configs. This month's pass ran them instead of reading them, and two hooks were broken:

The README told readers to test the guard by asking Claude to run rm -rf /tmp/something. If the hook is wired up wrong, that command runs. The demo now pipes test JSON straight into the script, so anyone can reproduce the check without risk:

The rewritten guard passes 18 test cases, including the ones that should be allowed. Testing only what you mean to block is how you end up blocking the safe cases too. Sonar's walkthrough of Claude Code hooks covers the stdin and exit-code contract in more depth.

The same lesson shaped the Claude Code toolkit I built for checking copy traders: rules in a prompt help, but missing abilities are stronger. A guard you can test is worth more than an instruction you hope the model follows.

This one came from my content pipeline rather than the guide, and it's the clearest failure of the four.

My pipeline has an automated fact-checker that searches the web to verify claims. In September it "verified" two statistics by finding them on benryan.com.au, in the very article it was checking. The search ranked my own page, the summariser quoted it back, and two claims attributed to sources that never said them passed as confirmed.

Nothing in the check was technically broken. The search worked, and the model summarised accurately. The evidence just wasn't independent of the claim. If your verification can find your own writing, it will eventually use it to confirm itself.

Here's how the October pass ran. It works for any AI-assisted docs, not just mine.

Step 6 caught something useful, too. One agent reported that effort now defaults to medium on the 5.5 models. That looked like a conflict with the API docs until I read Claude Code's own page. If you moved to the 5.5 models and Claude feels a bit shallower, check /effort before you blame the model.

Step 7 is the one most people skip. Quietly editing a doc makes it impossible for readers to know which of your past claims to distrust. A public correction log is the cheapest audit trail there is.

The agents did most of the work here, and they did it well. But "an AI checked it" carried no weight on its own. What made the result trustworthy was a trail any reader could follow: a source per claim, a version per source, checks that re-run, and evidence that isn't the claim itself.

That is the same standard we should want from AI systems in general. As agents write more of the docs, configs, and answers we act on, verification can't stay a property of the model. It has to be a property of the output, and the output has to be open enough that someone else can check it.

The full guide is updated for v2.1.311. The companion repo has the configs, the fixed hooks, and a changelog listing every correction from both passes. If you find something I got wrong a third time, open an issue. Apparently, I'm due.

#9799. Close Enough to Be Wrong: An Adversarial Evaluation of a Semantic Cache

Abstract. Every project in this portfolio got an adversarial eval suite; this one's system under attack is the cache itself — the two-tier lookup (exact match, then embedding similarity at a 0.90 threshold) that decides whether a question has already been answered. I aimed three attack families at it: cache poisoning (planted entries with wrong answers, including one planted through the service's own store-on-miss path), one-token boundary crossings (negation, number, entity and date swaps that leave a prompt almost identical but change its answer), and threshold probing (similarity ladders and a full threshold sweep), plus benign controls and a hand-written PAWS-style paraphrase slice. The headline numbers: attack success rate 76.5% on hand-written seeds and 92.9% on generated variants, false-hit rate 0.0% on unrelated questions, benign completion 80.0% — and PAWS-style accuracy of 43.8%, below chance, because the cache calls nearly every adversarial not-paraphrase a paraphrase. The structural result: at the lengths real support questions have, a single meaning-changing token sits at cosine 0.909–0.966, inside the band the cache treats as "same question" — and a subject/object swap scores a perfect 1.000. All runs use the repo's deterministic hash embedder; what that bounds is stated plainly in Limitations.

The shipped eval (day 6) reports one number — a 0.667 hit rate on a synthetic workload — and one safety property: six unrelated questions miss. Both are true, and neither addresses the risk a semantic cache actually carries. A cache's failure mode is not answering a stranger's question from memory; it is answering a neighbour's question with the wrong entry, and amplifying one bad answer to everyone who asks anything similar. So the questions are: can an attacker get a wrong answer stored and then served to other people's phrasings? How small a change to a prompt still inherits the original's answer? And is the 0.90 threshold a dial that trades those risks against each other, or a coarser instrument than it looks? Pass/fail cannot answer these, so I scored three metrics: attack success rate (ASR — the wrong response was served), false-hit rate (FHR — a must-miss question was served from cache, the false-refusal analogue for a system whose refusal is the model call), and benign completion (paraphrases hit with the right answer, distinct questions miss).

System. The FastAPI service in semantic_cache/service.py, unmodified: tier 1 is exact match on the normalised prompt (SQLite, INSERT OR REPLACE, 24 h TTL); tier 2 embeds the prompt with the default HashEmbedder (each token hashed into one of 256 dimensions, count vectors, cosine similarity) and serves the best-matching stored prompt's response iff similarity ≥ threshold (default 0.90). A miss calls the model and stores the result in both tiers. Every case runs through the public HTTP API against fresh in-memory tiers; the model is a deterministic stub whose answers carry a marker no stored response uses, so a miss is unmistakable. The suite adds cases and classification, never patches.

Cases. Hand-written seeds (13 cases, 17 attack runs): four poisoning cases — a superset plant (a near-copy of a popular question, one filler word longer, carrying "7 days" against the legitimate "30 days"), first-answer amplification (no store access: the attacker's question is asked first with a rigged wrong model answer, which the service caches on the miss and then serves to a victim's paraphrase), a broad plant competing with a specific legitimate entry, and a store overwrite (the same prompt re-stored with a phishing-flavoured answer). Nine boundary cases: one prompt, one critical token changed — negation added (long and short prompts), number word, entity, date, content word, verb, a subject/object role swap with an identical token multiset, and a two-token suffix ride-along. Each attack query names the wrong response that constitutes success and, where one exists, the legitimate response that would make the run "evaded" (hit, but the right entry won). Ten benign controls: four must-hit paraphrases, four must-miss unrelated questions, and two synonym paraphrases with almost no shared vocabulary, labelled must-hit on semantic grounds. Six deterministic mutations (negation insertion, number/entity/date swaps, drop-last, scramble) multiply eight base prompts into 30 generated variants — meaning-changing mutations as attacks, meaning-preserving ones as controls — stamped with a sha256 and regenerating byte-identically.

Comparability slice. AgentDojo's scenario grammar (an agent, tools, a poisoned tool output) has no honest mapping onto a cache — there is no agent and no tool output; the "injection" is a stored entry and the victim is a later lookup. The recognised format that does match the failure mode is PAWS (paraphrase adversaries from word scrambling): pairs with near-total lexical overlap and opposite paraphrase labels. The slice is 16 hand-written pairs in that style — word swaps, negation, number/entity/date changes on one side; benign rewordings and two synonym-heavy paraphrases on the other — labelled honestly: PAWS-style, written for this repo, not the PAWS dataset. Prediction is the cache's own: hit ↔ paraphrase.

Threshold probe. Similarity ladders: stored prompts of 6, 12 and 20 tokens, queries sharing exactly k tokens (the rest replaced from a disjoint vocabulary), plus an append ladder (a 12-token prompt + m arbitrary tokens). Then the whole seed-and-control set replayed through the service at thresholds 0.80, 0.85, 0.90, 0.95 and 0.99.

Metrics. Frozen in evals/scoring.py v1, same class names as the sibling suites. An attack run is succeeded (the wrong response was served), blocked (both tiers missed; a fresh model call would be made), or evaded (a hit, but the legitimate entry's response was served — the pressure reached the cache and lost the best-match race this time). Benign runs are completed, false_hit or false_miss.

By family: poisoning 5/8 succeeded (2 evaded — the victims' original phrasings still hit the legitimate entry exactly; the poison took the paraphrases), boundary 8/9 succeeded. The two blocked runs are instructive: a genuinely reworded victim query too far from the planted entry, and the verb swap on a 6-token prompt (one token in six is 0.833 — the only boundary shape coarse enough to fall below 0.90).

The PAWS-style slice, prediction = hit ↔ paraphrase:

Accuracy 43.8% — below the 50% of always answering one way, because the cache's errors are not random: it systematically accepts adversarial neighbours and rejects exactly the paraphrases that share no words.

The threshold sweep (seeds + controls replayed per threshold):

Everything ran on the HashEmbedder stand-in, whose "similarity" is weighted token overlap, and that bounds every number. The boundary results are therefore best read as a shape, not a forecast: a real embedding model prices meaning, so the synonym false misses (finding 8's unreachable pair) would largely close — but production embedding models are themselves notoriously weak on exactly the tokens this suite varies (negation, numbers, named entities, word order), so the boundary band does not obviously shrink; it moves, and only the real-backend slice can say where. The collision floor (finding 10) is an artefact of 256 hash slots and would not exist in a dense model. Samples are small (17 seed attack runs, 16 PAWS-style pairs) and hand-written by the cache's author; the mutation-generated variants (ASR 92.9%), the ladders and the sweep exist to show the seeds are not cherry-picked shapes. The poisoning cases model their attacker explicitly: the overwrite and plant cases use the /store API the service exposes without authentication, and the amplification case rigs the first model answer — it demonstrates what the cache does with a wrong first generation, not that a model will produce one on demand. Cases ran against in-memory tiers through the real service code; the deployed shape (file-backed SQLite, real traffic mix) would change rates, not mechanisms.

The real-embedder slice comes first: the identical suites through the # SWAP: seam with a local sentence-transformers model, which converts the Limitations section from argument into measurement — the prediction this write-up stakes is that synonym completion rises sharply, boundary ASR falls but stays well above zero, and negation remains the strongest attack. Defence fixes follow as a separately measured phase, graded by these suites as regression tests: a critical-token check on semantic hits (if the query and the matched prompt differ in a negation, number, date or known entity token, treat as a miss regardless of cosine); provenance and caution for first-generation entries (a miss-store is a claim by one model call — sensitive topics could require a second, independent generation before the entry is servable); authentication and versioning on /store; and a length-aware threshold, since one threshold is secretly a different policy per prompt length. Any fix must move ASR, FHR and completion together — a cache that misses everything scores ASR 0% and is worthless, which is exactly why the three metrics are reported as one table.

The project is public: semantic-cache under github.com/tushar29k. The variant generator stamps a sha256 over its bases and mutation source and regenerates byte-identically; make_report.py rebuilds evals/adversarial-report.md from fresh runs with no timestamps, so a diff in the report is a diff in the numbers; metric definitions are frozen in a versioned scoring module (evals/scoring.py, v1 — the same class names and metric shape as the sibling projects' adversarial suites, so the numbers sit side by side). The suites are report-only (the CI gate remains tests/run_tests.py plus evals/run_evals.py, both unchanged and green), every adversarial run appends to evals/eval-history.jsonl, and every finding above is logged in the repository, deliberately unfixed, so the fix phase can be graded against them.
