#9798. Build a Hook Generator in Python That Checks the First Three Seconds

A script can be short on the page and still miss the opening shot. “Before you replace your old desk mat, try this” feels concise until you read it aloud, pause before the reveal, and discover the product has not appeared yet.

This tutorial builds a deliberately small Python hook generator: three templates, a transparent scoring function, and a few tests. It does not predict virality. It catches avoidable production problems before someone records a batch of openings that are too long, too vague, or based on claims the product cannot support.

I work on UGCfy AI. The code here is a standalone teaching implementation, not a copy of its production system, an unofficial API client, or an ad-performance model. The examples use a hypothetical desk mat. None of the scores below come from an advertising campaign.

Start with a brief, not a prompt that says “make this viral.” For our fictional desk mat, the brief contains a problem: a mat that slides while someone types. The desired outcome is a steadier keyboard. The demonstration is a side-by-side push on the actual desk. The product team still needs to establish that the advertised mat does what the demonstration implies.

The brief should also list forbidden claims. No invented customer counts. No “sold out again” without inventory evidence. No first-person testimonial unless the speaker actually had that experience. A template can make a fabricated statement sound casual; that does not make it acceptable.

I keep a candidate's wording separate from its review flags. The program cannot look at a sentence and know whether the product really passed a test. Someone has to check the evidence and mark the claim supported. Making that judgment explicit is better than hiding it inside a keyword match that rewards any hook containing “proven.”

For a production tool, store the evidence reference next to the flag: a test recording, a reviewed product specification, or an approved claim document. A boolean is sufficient for this tutorial, but it is not a substitute for a traceable review.

There is no language-model dependency in this version. Templates make it easy to see where every phrase came from and to test the same brief repeatedly. That is useful when the goal is learning the pipeline rather than maximizing variety.

Those templates cover a problem call-out, a desired outcome, and an interruption before an action. They are structures, not guarantees of quality. A poorly chosen problem will remain a poorly chosen problem after the function adds a question mark.

Notice the grammar contract. problem should be a noun phrase such as “a sliding desk mat,” not a complete sentence. action should be a verb phrase such as “replace your desk mat.” If the caller passes “your mat keeps sliding,” the first template becomes awkward. In a larger tool, document that contract or store structured phrase types instead of accepting arbitrary strings.

The tokenizer is intentionally English-oriented. It counts contractions and hyphenated expressions as one token. That choice keeps the example consistent, but it does not establish actual pronunciation length. A long product name, a number, or an unfamiliar acronym can take longer to say than its token count suggests.

A word cap is only a rough timing proxy. Here the configurable speaking-rate assumption is 160 words per minute. At that assumed pace, eight words occupy three seconds before any pauses. That is arithmetic, not a measured average for creators or a platform rule.

The estimate is 60 × word_count / words_per_minute. A different speaker, language, or delivery changes the budget. If the creator pauses for emphasis or the opening needs a visual demonstration, fewer spoken words may be appropriate. Do not speed the voice up merely to satisfy the score.

I assign forty points to fitting the estimated window, twenty-five to specificity, twenty to having a matching opening shot, and fifteen to supported claims. Those weights are editorial choices. There is no training set behind them. The full explanation travels with the score so a reviewer can disagree with a rule rather than treating a number as authority.

Eligibility is separate from ranking. Unsupported claims are not rescued by a good length score. An empty string is also ineligible even if someone has accidentally checked the “supported” box. Only compare eligible candidates, and still review them before recording.

Specificity and visual availability are human inputs here. Passing True is an annotation, not something the function discovered. That distinction matters when showing results to a teammate who might otherwise assume the program watched the footage or understood the product.

The complete executable file is saved as hooks.py beside this draft. I ran it using the following hypothetical brief:

For this fixture, all three review flags were deliberately set to true. That makes it a test of generation and timing arithmetic, not an independent review of a real product.

The third candidate fails the timing check. That is useful behavior: generation does not force every output through the same length mold, and scoring gives a specific reason to revise one. “Desk mat sliding? Try this.” is a possible edit, but it needs its own read-through and matching shot.

The script also asserts that an unsupported claim is ineligible and that an empty hook is ineligible. Those assertions passed in the same run. They establish a few code invariants; they say nothing about click-through rate, early retention, cost per thousand impressions, or sales.

A score of one hundred means only that a candidate satisfied this rule set under the supplied annotations. It does not mean a perfect advertisement. Two candidates can tie while producing very different experiences on screen.

For “Still dealing with a sliding desk mat?”, the first frame should make the sliding mat legible. If the video opens on a face, then cuts to a wide room view, then finally shows the mat, the spoken line and the visual are competing instead of cooperating.

Write a tiny shot specification beside each candidate. Record the first image, the action, any on-screen text, and the point where the product becomes identifiable. A useful specification might say: close crop on typing hands; the old mat shifts; no text covering the movement; the replacement enters in the next shot.

Test the opening without sound. Can a viewer identify the problem? Then listen without the picture. Does the sentence still make sense? You do not need both channels to explain everything independently, but an essential detail should not depend on tiny text that disappears before anyone can read it.

Finally record a rough take. Use the actual speaker and intended delivery. A stopwatch or waveform replaces the speaking-rate estimate at this stage. If the line takes too long, cut words or redesign the reveal. The point of the estimate is to make that correction cheap, not to overrule the recording.

If you want a wider candidate pool without maintaining templates, UGCfy AI's hook generator takes a product description and platform choice and returns hook suggestions with their associated psychological angles. It is an alternative writing surface; the review process still belongs to you.

Do not treat any generated first-person story, social-proof line, or before-and-after statement as automatically approved. The same evidence check applies whether the words came from a template, a language model, a freelance writer, or a brainstorm in a meeting. The tool proposes language; your brief determines what you can responsibly say.

Shortlist openings that communicate genuinely different angles. Changing “still” to “always” rarely teaches as much as comparing a visible problem against a clear desired outcome. Keep the script body and offer consistent enough that you can interpret the opening change.

Define the outcome before the test. Early retention can help diagnose attention; qualified visits or purchases answer different business questions. A dramatic opening may earn a pause while attracting the wrong audience. Record both the attention signal and the downstream outcome relevant to the campaign.

Keep the platform's actual metric definition in your notes. A view is not interchangeable across placements or reporting interfaces. Avoid declaring a winner from a handful of events, and do not interpret unequal automated delivery as a clean randomized experiment. The delivery system may be selecting audiences as well as allocating impressions.

The practical result is a short audit trail: the brief, generated wording, reviewer flags, estimated duration, recorded duration, first shot, and observed campaign results. The Python score belongs near the beginning of that trail. Its job is to reject obvious problems before production, not to impersonate evidence from the end.

#9797. Transformers Model Integration Contracts

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:

It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:

It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

#9796. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing.

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

As both writing assistants are great in their own way, you need to choose the one that suits you best.

Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.

Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.

I use the paid versions of both Grammarly and Pro Writing Aid. Both of them have issues:- Grammarly IS more focused on nonfiction than fiction. If you're writing fiction, you may find Grammarly's insistence on "Conciseness" annoying. They seem to want to take the soul out of your writing, which is fine for a corporate report or technical manual, but not for your Great American Novel.- Grammarly pushes features on users that are not ready for prime time. It doesn't matter that you never agreed to be a beta tester for them; you get to do it anyway.- Pro Writing Aid actually counts the occurrences of words in your document and tells you when a word has been overused compared to published literature. Grammarly, on the other hand, seems hell-bent to remove certain words that it has deemed overused from the language, whether or not they're actually overused in your document.- Grammarly's Clarity function is simply horrible. It mangles sentences and changes their meaning. Sometimes the result of its suggestion is unintelligible garbage.- Grammarly allows you to turn off some checks, but not all of them. Unfortunately, the ones you cannot turn off are some of the most irritating (such as that horrible "Clarity"). On the other hand, Pro Writing Aid lets you choose which checks you use.- Pro Writing Aid has a mediocre command of American English (it's a British product). The app insists on rules of grammar and spelling that are outright wrong, per Merriam-Webster, the Chicago Manual of Style, and modern usage as shown by Google Books Ngram. At one point, Pro Writing Aid insisted that American English did not include the words "holiday" and "autumn," that "vacation" and "fall" must be used instead.- Pro Writing Aid's rules for commas are 100 percent consistent with the way I learned them in high school--50 years ago! They do not reflect modern usage. Grammarly is much better at this.- Pro Writing Aid seems to waste their limited resources on tweaking their UI. Their UI most definitely could use improvement, but these changes are not great improvements; they only serve to confuse users. Their resources would be better spent fixing the many functional problems in their app.- Some of Pro Writing Aid's checks are completely useless, as they do not take context into consideration. For example, an ordinary word would not be capitalized as part of a narrative, but would be as part of a title (for example, "professor." But if you capitalize correctly for context, Pro Writing Aid dings you for "Inconsistent capitalization." Similar issues exist with hyphenation consistency check.Each of these applications has its strengths as well as considerable weaknesses. I will say that both of them are light-years better than the execrable grammar checker in Microsoft Word, but that's damning with faint praise.

#9795. SealedBench: A Protocol for Freezing AI Benchmarks Before the Questions Are Known

A frozen model manifest, a generator sealed with drand, and an Arweave record anyone can use to rebuild the exam and check its scores.

On 2026-10-17, a bundle carrying my encrypted generator reached an Arweave block. The generator was sealed to a drand round that had not been published yet. I wrote that program, so I knew it would produce integer word problems, short Python programs, and shortest-path questions. I did not know which ones. The questions depended on a beacon the drand network would publish later, at round 33170212, on 2026-10-18T09:00:00Z.

When the round arrived, the same beacon value unlocked the program and seeded it. Four open-weight models answered 360 completions each: 240 on newly generated questions and 120 on a frozen set of public GSM8K items.

But the first two batches I ran should not be cited, and it is worth saying why, because the reason is the most useful thing in this article.

The first batch, b1, was valid under its own release record. Its manifest bound the ciphertext with a SHA-256 hash, but it never bound the ciphertext's transaction ID. Calling that check a pass would be a mistake, and it is WEAK. The v2 protocol exists partly to close that gap.

The second batch, b2, fixed the binding and then failed on the grader. The rule I sealed said an integer answer counts only when the last line is #### followed by nothing but the number. llama.cpp writes its end-of-text marker onto that same line, as #### 392 [end of text]. The registered grader threw the whole line away. Most of b2's arithmetic and GSM8K scores measure that rejection, not the rate at which models produced correct integers.

The ciphertext was already sealed by then, and the grader could not be changed in place. That constraint is the entire point of the protocol, and it applies to me too. So I made b3: a new commitment, sealed before its own round, with the normalization written into the scorer the manifest hashes.

So if you want a number from this project, take one from b3, and take the registered primary accuracy, which counts an answer as wrong when it cannot be parsed and wrong when the output was truncated. Its index transaction is vlVlUfyBn4IUmbXjkSX8079QuySP-Qqr8rN8TbivzTg. That index was published after the run. It is a convenient entry point, not evidence: the evidence that the generator existed before the round is the earlier ciphertext and manifest.

Public benchmarks leak. Once the questions are online, a high score may only mean the model has seen them.

A private test set looks like the fix, but it hands the same power to one person: whoever writes, stores, selects and reports the questions. That person includes the evaluator, which is me. If I can see the scores and then quietly change the seed, the prompt, the model file, or simply decide which batch to tell you about, I can aim the headline wherever I want.

SealedBench tries to pin all of that down in advance. The generator, the model hashes, the prompts, the runtime settings and the scoring code are bound to one future beacon round. Unless drand's operators reach a threshold and collude to compute that round early, I cannot read the beacon before it is published. If the network stops, the batch never opens; that is the other half of the bargain. After the round, anyone can rebuild the questions from the Arweave record and re-score the answers I published.

Here is every move I could make, and what I gave up in advance to make it visible.

Ciphertext and manifest on Arweave before the round

Check L1 block time, not the upload receipt

A hash cannot show which process wrote a file

Encryption cannot force me to publish answers

The manifest freezes the drand chain hash and public key, the release round, the seed rule, a SHA-256 for every GGUF, the llama.cpp commit and build flags, the prompts, the decoding settings, the grader and the reporting policy. Every batch uses quicknet chain 52db9ba70e0cc0f6eaf7803dd07447a1f5477735fd3f661792ba94600c84e971, genesis at unix 1692803367, period 3 seconds.

The generator is sealed to that round with drand time-lock encryption (tlock). The ciphertext and the manifest go up through the Turbo bundler. A receipt is not a commitment. The commitment is the L1 block.

Under the v2 rule a batch is valid only if the block holding its bundle is timestamped no later than unlock_unix − 600, the bundle ID appears in that block, and the data item's bytes hash to the committed SHA-256. Height, timestamp and block hash must agree on two independent gateways, and my own gateway ario.zigza.xyz does not count as either one. b1 used an earlier, simpler rule: manifest and ciphertext had to be in an L1 block before the release round, and a miss made the batch invalid, which I would still have had to report.

After the round, the beacon signature is checked against quicknet's fixed public key. The same beacon both decrypts the generator and enters the seed. One value doing two jobs is not two independent draws, and I do not claim otherwise.

b1's seed is a SHA-256 over a domain string, the chain hash, the round in decimal and the beacon randomness, with hex fields lowercased first. The exact sentence is in b1's manifest. v2 batches add a 32-byte secret stored inside the ciphertext, and hash length-prefixed fields: domain, chain hash, round, signature bytes and that secret. The JSON randomness field is not an input; it must still equal the SHA-256 of the signature. I chose the secret. It does not let me list the questions before the beacon exists. A successful tle -d only shows the ciphertext opens under the signature it was sealed to. The BLS check against the fixed public key is a separate step.

There is one specific gap in v1 worth naming. The November capsule cap and b1 share the same plaintext tarball, SHA-256 e054f1ab7824fde33e6ac399252098cf25c29815ff4ffacabbd311da05eac9c2. Once b1 opened, that program was public. Until 2026-11-15 the unknown is the beacon, not the program. v2 still hides its questions, because the secret sits inside the ciphertext.

Every family has a program for an oracle, so grading is code and not a judge model. arith_word produces two-to-five-step integer word problems; the oracle is a function of the sampling parameters, and the prompt contains no answer line. code_output produces short Python programs with no imports and no input, run in an interpreter with a step budget; the oracle is their stdout. graph_path asks for the weight of a shortest path on a random connected graph with edge weights from 1 to 9, always between nodes at least two edges apart; the oracle is Dijkstra.

The entropy check ran the generator over 1000 seeds and got 1000 distinct question sets, with 128,816 distinct prompts. That shows the seed changes the questions. It does not show the families are fair, or that they look unlike anything in training data. One caveat I want on the record: that check ran with a stand-in secret, not the sealed one, so it measures the generator's spread and not the exact bytes b2 and b3 committed.

All four models are official Q8_0 GGUFs, hashed locally against the published LFS object IDs before sealing:

Falcon3-1B is weak on purpose. It is a low anchor that makes a difficulty shift easier to see.

The runtime is llama.cpp v0.7.0, commit 620d2225cc436ab0b001e3200e590e3b286ef9ab, built CPU-only with AVX-512 on a Ryzen 7 7700 in a cgroup of about six CPUs and 18 GiB. Decoding is greedy: temperature 0, top-k 1, top-p 1, min-p 0, seed 42, -t 6 -b 2048 -ub 512.

Thread count and batch size are in the manifest because they change the output bytes. Repeated runs at -t 6 were byte-identical for all four models. Dropping to -t 4 changed 2 of 10 Qwen outputs. Changing to -b 512 -ub 128 changed Qwen, Gemma and Falcon. Ministral matched in all three comparisons. After release I replayed Qwen's first ten exam items: 10/10 byte-identical on b1, 10/10 on b2, 10/10 on b3. That is one model on one machine. Generating and grading are ordinary deterministic programs. I am not claiming your GPU would produce the same bytes.

120 arith, 60 code, 60 graph, plus GSM8K-test 0..119

The same scores.json carries a block called posthoc_sentinel_normalization, labelled POST-HOC with registered_primary false. It keeps the truncation rule on raw stdout and applies b3's normalization before the integer and code rules. There Qwen scores 73/80 on arithmetic and 77/80 on GSM8K. That is a reconstruction, not the score b2 promised to report.

b3 pins sealedbench/v2/grade.py and sealedbench/v2/grade_b3.py. The grader SHA-256 eab22119c837f790f900989ce7d3c8700635ad7881204ffc90079d800854b290 is a hash over both files sorted by path, not the hash of grade_b3.py alone. The registered normalization strips trailing ASCII whitespace, removes one trailing [end of text] if present, then strips again. Truncation is decided before that, on raw stdout. b3 has no post-hoc block. Its manifest is _aZZOYmKQr9awEhsmKew9J4sAHyDnfZoo1Pq1NYXOVk and its ciphertext MU3l3e_pbboAuVH8dtiLJP4XMGKGaFR530w-TauzteM.

v2 release files leave batch_valid unset. Their inclusion records put every sealed item's L1 time before that batch's own deadline. b2 and cap2 share bundle VWHJrEUcS-d9EXMzzJr9k6Qr2WKQLR9iwiMfm4nglgo, height 2023391, 2026-10-17T20:05:59Z. b3 and cap3 share J67Udct-eWBqCnNfoT9c_d0baY48io8tHlJ8uD_ZVys, height 2023739, 2026-10-18T08:11:02Z.

Primary accuracy, with invalid and truncated answers counted as wrong:

The Wilson 95% intervals behind the two columns in the figure, rounded to three decimals from the wilson95 arrays: Qwen arithmetic [0.800, 0.940] and GSM8K [0.895, 0.987]; Gemma [0.168, 0.355] and [0.232, 0.434]; Ministral [0.846, 0.965] and [0.713, 0.883]; Falcon [0.478, 0.689] and [0.179, 0.368].

At n=80 near one half, a Wilson interval is roughly 11 points wide. A gap inside that width is the difference between two unmatched sets of questions. The fresh and public items differ in wording, length and format.

Calling that gap contamination would need a control this run does not have. One overlap should be stated plainly: Phase 1 had already run the models on GSM8K-test items 0..49, and b3's reference set covers 0..79, so the first 50 reference items were familiar ground before b3 was sealed. Nothing in this run separates that familiarity from the ordinary difficulty difference between two unmatched question sets.

Two cells deserve more than a headline. Qwen's graph score is 9/30, and 21 of those 30 outputs were truncated; across that family it produced 15 distinct answers, against a uniform-guess baseline of 0.067. Gemma's arithmetic is 20/80 with 60 invalid, and all 20 that parsed were correct; it produced 67 distinct answers, against a uniform-guess baseline of 0.015.

I measured four Turbo bundles. The 20 probes from the first day are one bundle, not 20 latency samples. Latency here is the L1 block timestamp minus the earliest receipt time in that bundle.

The probes are 800 bytes each, sealed with tle v1.2.0 to rounds between 1176 and 1403 seconds after upload. Both the Go tool and tlock-js 0.9.0 refused to decrypt early, in 40 of 40 attempts. All 20 Turbo receipts verified. All 60 RFC 3161 timestamps from FreeTSA, DigiCert and Sectigo verified with openssl ts -verify. After the unlock, 20 of 20 probes decrypted in both tools and matched their plaintext hashes. FreeTSA's genTime landed a median 76.2 seconds after the Turbo receipt.

A GraphQL poller pointed at arweave.net ran for three hours and got HTTP 429 every time, observing nothing. Serving bytes, being in a block and being indexed are three different states. The commitment is the block. When arweave.net returns 404, the honest output is UNKNOWN.

Figure 3 — receipt-to-inclusion ECDF, one point per bundle, n=4. article/fig/fig3_inclusion_ecdf.png.

The repository is https://github.com/zigengZ/sealedbench, released as v1.0.0. You need Python 3.12 and Node.js 22. Leave SEALEDBENCH_ROOT unset.

Exit code 0 is PASS, 1 is a hard failure, and 2 is UNKNOWN, INVALID or WEAK. HTTP 404, 429 and timeouts all count as UNKNOWN. The command only reads gateways; it never uploads. It checks the published bytes, the inclusion deadline, the beacon signature and the grader hash, re-scores the published outputs, then decrypts the local ciphertext and rebuilds the question files. v2 requires https://ar-io.dev and https://turbo-gateway.com to agree. https://arweave.net takes no part in this check.

On 2026-10-24 a fresh clone of the release candidate printed RESULT PASS, exit code 0, in 26.15 seconds. drand is an assumption. A threshold of operators could collude to compute a future round early. If the network stopped, the capsules would never open.

Closed models are outside this protocol. I cannot see their weights or their serving stack.

#9794. How to make a scanned PDF small enough to email

Six pages photographed on a phone and turned into one PDF can weigh more than the mail service will accept. Many stop at 25 MB, and an attachment grows by about a third when it is encoded for mail, so a 30 MB file is well over. The usual fix is an online compressor, which means uploading the document, a lease in the example below, to someone else's server. The PDF Editor in the osFoundry desktop app does it on the computer instead, in three steps. The example is a 6-page lease scanned on a phone, a made-up document for this demonstration, and it goes from 30.7 MB to 1.0 MB.

Open the PDF in the PDF Editor (Canvas, then PDF Editor), click All tools, then Compress a PDF, then Advanced optimization. The PDF Optimizer dialog has an Audit space usage button at the bottom left. It adds the file up by kind of content.

For the lease, Images are 32,225,071 of 32,227,412 bytes, 99.99%. The text and everything else weigh a few kilobytes. Each page is a photo about 3,000 pixels wide, and the photos are the file. This is typical of PDFs made from phone photos, and it is why a text document exported from a word processor is tiny while a scan of the same page is not. If the audit shows something else taking the space, shrinking the images will not help much. Click OK to return to the dialog.

The dialog's Images tab shows the settings. By default, color and grayscale images drawn at more than 225 ppi are resampled to 150 ppi and saved as JPEG at Medium quality.

The ppi that matters is how densely the page draws the image, not what the camera reported. A 3,024-pixel-wide photo drawn across an 8.5-inch page is about 356 ppi, a lot more than reading needs, and 150 is plenty for text on a screen or on a printout. The line under the settings says that each image is measured where the pages draw it, and that an image is replaced only if the new version is smaller, so a file that was already small is not made bigger. The defaults were right for this file, so nothing was changed. Click OK.

The editor saves a new file next to the original, named like the original with "(optimized)" added, here en (optimized).pdf. The copy is 1.0 MB, against 30.7 MB for the original, about 97% smaller. The original file is not changed.

Open the copy and zoom in. Each page is now an image of 1275 × 1700 pixels, 150 ppi on the page, instead of 3024 × 4032.

Read the contract text at 125% and compare it with the original before sending: this is lossy compression, and the check takes seconds. At 150 ppi the printed text stays sharp. If a document has fine print or small handwriting, the same dialog can be run again from the original with a higher ppi, for example 200, to trade some size for detail.

The 1.0 MB copy is attached to the mail; the 30.7 MB original stays in its folder.

The PDF Editor is part of the osFoundry desktop app, which is free for macOS, Windows and Linux from the download page, and it works on files that stay on the computer; the local-first page explains what that means.

#9793. CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency

CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where new models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:

Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:

-k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

#9792. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)


If you want to pay online, you need to register an account and provide credit card information. If you don't have a credit card, you can pay with bank transfer. With the rise of cryptocurrencies, these methods may become old.

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain. 

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

So, What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

  • Blockchain collects information in “blocks”.
  • A block has a storage capacity, and once it's used up, it can be closed and linked to a previously served block.
  • Blocks form chains, which are called “Blockchains.”
  • More information will be added to the block with the most content until its capacity is full. The process repeats itself.
  • Each block in the chain has an exact timestamp and can't be changed.

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

How does blockchain work?

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

Here’s how it works:

  • Someone or a computer will transacts
  • The transaction is transmitted throughout the network.
  • A network of computers can confirm the transaction.
  • When it is confirmed a transaction is added to a block
  • The blocks are linked together to create a history.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

  • A new transaction is added to the system. It is then relayed to a network of computers located around the world. The computers then solve equations to ensure the authenticity of the transaction.
  • Once a transaction is confirmed, it is placed in a block after the confirmation. All of the blocks are chained together to create a permanent history of every transaction.

How are Blockchains used?

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

What is Blockchain Decentralization?

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Pros and Cons of Blockchain

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages. 

Pros

  • Accuracy is increased because there is no human involvement in the verification process.
  • One of the great things about decentralization is that it makes information harder to tamper with.
  • Safe, private, and easy transactions
  • Provides a banking alternative and safe storage of personal information

Cons

  • Data storage has limits.
  • The regulations are always changing, as they differ from place to place.
  • It has a risk of being used for illicit activities 

Frequently Asked Questions About Blockchain

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Is Blockchain a cryptocurrency?

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Is it possible for Blockchain to be hacked?

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

What is the most prominent blockchain company?

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Who owns Blockchain?

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

What is the difference between Bitcoin and Blockchain technology?

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency 

What is the difference between Blockchain and a Database?

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Final Saying

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9791. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:

#9790. A Practitioner's Field Guide to Marketing Engineering

Growth marketer, 10+ years in SaaS, AI and Web3. I build AI systems that do marketing work so one person can run what used to take a team.

Growth marketer, 10+ years in SaaS, AI and Web3. I build AI systems that do marketing work so one person can run what used to take a team.

Growth marketer, 10+ years in SaaS, AI and Web3. I build AI systems that do marketing work so one person can run what used to take a team.

My name is Kristina Vislianska. I'm a growth marketer with 10+ years in B2B and B2C SaaS, AI, and Web3, and for the last couple of years, most of what I ship isn't campaigns. It's systems that run campaigns.

At some point, recruiters and founders started calling this "marketing engineering." I had to Google it. Turns out I'd been doing it for a while; I just called it "building stuff so I don't lose my mind doing the same thing every Monday."

This guide is for marketers who want to build, founders who want to hire someone who builds, and engineers who wonder what marketers are doing with their Claude or Codex Pro Max. Everything here comes from systems I built and ran, including the ones that broke.

Marketing engineering turns repeatable go-to-market work into software, combining marketing judgment with engineering skills. Its systems listen to the market, turn what they hear into content, distribute it, and learn from the results. A marketing engineer's output is not a campaign. It's the machine that produces campaigns.

The deliverable is a monitor, a pipeline, an agent or a feedback loop. Something that keeps working when you close your laptop.

And no, it's not "marketing that uses AI tools." Asking ChatGPT for ten hooks is using a tool. Marketing engineering starts when the work keeps running without you typing.

The title keeps changing. A few years ago it was "growth hacker," then "marketing technologist," now "GTM engineer" and "marketing engineer." Honestly, I don't think the title will survive. The skill will.

Marketing ops runs the machine. A GTM engineer builds the machine for sales. A marketing engineer builds the machine for attention. The three roles overlap, and the job titles are still a mess, so here's how I draw the lines.

Marketing ops keeps the existing stack working: clean CRM data, campaign setup, attribution reports. Success looks like data you can trust.

GTM engineers build the revenue engine for sales: enrichment, outbound sequences, lead routing. Success looks like meetings booked and pipeline.

Marketing engineers build the systems that create and distribute marketing: listening tools, content pipelines, community monitors, AI search presence, agents. Success looks like reach, citations in AI answers, and how much one person can run.

Think of a restaurant. Marketing ops keeps the kitchen clean and the orders flowing. The GTM engineer builds the delivery system that gets food to customers who already ordered. The marketing engineer builds the thing that makes people walk past and want to come in. Usually a marketing engineer combines the roles of a whole team of specialists. I like to call them the king of agents and systems.

Everything I've built fits into one of five layers: Listen, Understand, Make, Ship and Learn. I call it the marketing engineering loop, because what you learn at the end changes what you listen for at the start.

Here's the thing most teams get wrong. They start with Make, because "AI writes posts" is the obvious use case. But content volume was never the bottleneck. In my experience the biggest gains sit in Listen and Learn. Listening finds the moments worth acting on. Learning tells you which of your actions actually mattered.

Automate tasks that repeat often and are safe to get wrong. For tasks that repeat often but happen in public, let the machine draft and keep a human on the send button. I call this the frequency × risk matrix.

The most common mistake I see is automating whatever is easiest to automate. That's how you end up with a bot that confidently replies to a grieving customer with a discount code. Two questions work much better: how often does this task repeat, and how bad is it if the machine gets it wrong in front of people? The answer is a split: the machine finds and drafts, a person approves and sends.

Theory is nice, but you came here for the real stuff. Here's one system for each layer of the loop, with what it taught me.

Situation. I wanted to find advisory clients without cold pitching. I hate cold pitching, and so does everyone receiving it. The best moment to talk to a founder is when they post "we just raised" or complain that growth has stalled. Those posts disappear from the feed in hours.

What I built. A radar that searches Threads for pain-point phrases in English and trigger phrases in Ukrainian, like "we raised" or "we got our first revenue." For every match it drafts a reply and pings me in Telegram or email. I read it, rewrite it if needed, and post it myself. The system never posts on its own, and nobody gets a pitch in the first message.

What it taught me. Listening is the cheapest layer to automate and the most valuable. Timing beats copy.

Situation. At an AI workflow automation platform, we were selling agents to small service businesses in seven verticals. To sell to them, we needed to know which tools they already use and what actually makes them swear at their phones.

What I built. A research system that produces three things per vertical: an integration map of the software they already use, a pain-point file built from scraped Reddit threads and classified by an LLM, and ready-made agent templates that solve the top pain with the tools they already have. The research didn't just shape the message. It turned into the product itself: the templates.

What changed. Cost per lead dropped by 80%. Instead of guessing, we shipped 7 agent templates, one per vertical, each built around a pain owners described in their own words. Our one-size-fits-all pitch was gone.

What it taught me. Research is the cheapest way to lower acquisition cost. Before you spend another dollar on ads, find out how your buyers describe their pain. And the same research that shapes your message tells the product team what to build next.

Situation. We needed explainer videos for all seven verticals. We had no video team and no budget to hire one.

What I built. A pipeline where a script goes in and a finished video comes out. The script is split into lines. A voice API generates the voiceover for each line as a separate audio file. Remotion, a React framework for video, renders each scene, and the length of each audio file sets the length of its scene. The on-screen graphics come from a custom skill that holds our whole design system, so every frame follows our brand style guide.

What changed. Seven verticals covered without hiring a single editor. One agent turns a script into a finished, on-brand video in 15 minutes. The pipeline produced 5 videos a day at under $1 each, a fraction of what an agency charges.

What it taught me. When a video costs less than a dollar and 15 minutes, it stops being a project and becomes an experiment. You can test messages in video the way you test headlines. The bottleneck moves from production to knowing what to say, which is exactly why the Listen and Understand layers come first.

Situation. Outreach on X works best when you show up in the right conversation at the right moment. Doing that by hand means scrolling for hours, hoping to catch the one post where someone describes exactly the problem you solve. And by the time you've written a good reply, the moment is gone.

What I built. A browser extension for X that finds outreach opportunities by keywords and trigger phrases, like someone announcing a launch, asking for a tool recommendation or complaining about a problem. When it finds a match, a ready-made prompt system drafts the reply for me in my voice. I read it, tweak it if needed, and send it myself. Every reply gets logged, so the system learns which triggers and formats actually start conversations.

What changed. 20 targeted replies a day, without losing my whole morning. Instead of scrolling for an hour to find two good posts, I review a list of drafts, each tied to a real trigger, and spend my time only on the human part. The logs show which triggers start conversations and which just collect polite likes, so the keyword list gets sharper every week.

What it taught me. Automating Learn isn't about saving time. It's about running enough experiments to see what a platform rewards and punishes. A handful of manual replies will never show you that.

Tools change every few months. These six principles haven't changed across anything I've built, and most of them I learned by breaking something.

You don't need a computer science degree. You climb four rungs: Operator, Assembler, Builder and Architect. Each one needs a different skill, and most marketers get stuck between the second and the third.

Full honesty: I don't write Python from memory. I build with Claude Code and Cursor. What I can do is read the code, understand why it broke, and explain to the AI what to fix. That's the real skill.

The jump from Assembler to Builder isn't about learning to write code. It's about learning to read it well enough to tell why it stopped working at 3 a.m.

Your best first project? Your most boring weekly task. Build the system, put yourself on the send button, and measure what you learn, not the time you save. That's the whole discipline in miniature.

Is marketing engineering the same as growth hacking? No. Growth hacking was about finding clever tactics. Marketing engineering is about building durable systems that run those tactics repeatedly and learn from the results.

Do marketing engineers need to know how to code? They need to read code, not necessarily write it from scratch. With AI coding tools like Claude Code or Cursor, the bottleneck is understanding what broke and why.

What tools do marketing engineers use? Usually LLM APIs, Python or JavaScript, scrapers, no-code automation tools, voice and video AI, etc. The specific tools matter less than the loop they form.

What is the difference between a marketing engineer and a GTM engineer? A GTM engineer builds systems that turn buying signals into sales pipeline. A marketing engineer builds systems that turn market signals into reach, content and visibility.

What should a company automate first in marketing? Tasks that repeat weekly and are safe to get wrong, like monitoring, research and reporting. Public-facing tagive me sks like replies and outreach should be drafted by machines and sent by humans.

Will AI replace marketers? AI replaces repetitive marketing tasks, not marketing judgment. Deciding what to automate, what to say and when a process is broken is still a human job.

Marketing engineering is not about making more content faster. AI already solved that, and honestly, the internet didn't need more of it. It's about building systems that know where to listen, what to say, where to ship it and what to learn from it, while you keep the judgment.

The tools will keep changing. The judgment about what's worth automating is the part that stays yours.

Which layer of the loop have you automated already, and which one do you think is overrated? Tell me in the comments. I read all of them, without a bot.

Growth marketer, 10+ years in SaaS, AI and Web3. I build AI systems that do marketing work so one person can run what used to take a team.

#9788. Scenario Testing vs Single Endpoint Testing

Posted on Nov 8 • Originally published at powerduck.com

Quick answer: A single endpoint test verifies one request in isolation, checking its own status and response against a fixed expectation. A scenario test verifies an ordered chain of connected requests, where values pass between steps and assertions run at each stage. They answer different questions: whether one call works, and whether the whole flow it belongs to works.

The core distinction is scope. A single endpoint test treats one operation as the entire subject, while a scenario treats the business flow as the subject.

Isolated tests are fast and precise. They pin the behavior of one operation, make failures easy to locate because there is only one call, and work well as a broad regression net across many endpoints. When you change one handler, a single endpoint test tells you quickly whether that handler still responds as expected.

The limit is that real behavior rarely lives in one call. A request that returns 200 on its own can hand back an id or token that the next call rejects, and the isolated test never sees that break. It also cannot tell you whether the steps connect in the right order.

A scenario models the dependencies between calls. A login step extracts a token, a create step uses it and returns an id, and a read step confirms the resource exists. Assertions at each stage catch the failure that no isolated test can: a chain that breaks between steps.

This is how a scenario catches a 200 response that still breaks the contract or a later step, because it reads the whole flow rather than one answer.

The two complement rather than compete. Use single endpoint tests for wide, fast coverage of individual operations, and add scenario tests for the critical business flows that span several calls. A suite with only isolated calls misses broken chains; a suite with only scenarios is slow and gives less precise coverage of every endpoint.

A practical rule is to keep the isolated layer wide enough that every operation has at least one check, then reserve scenarios for the handful of flows where a break costs money or blocks a user, such as signup, checkout, and billing. That keeps the suite fast while still guarding the chains that matter.

Scenarios stay outside the OpenAPI document, with no x-scenarios keys, and they run against real connected requests rather than mocks. A mock replays fixed answers and does not verify the backend.

Powerduck keeps both views available, so you can confirm a single operation and then verify the connected flow that depends on it, with per-step evidence rather than a single green label.

Should I replace single endpoint tests with scenarios? No. Keep isolated tests for fast, broad coverage of each operation, and use scenarios for the multi-step business flows. They cover different failure modes.

Can a single endpoint test catch a broken chain? No. It only sees one call, so it cannot detect a value that a later step rejects or an ordering problem across requests.

Do scenarios share state between steps? Yes. A value from one response is extracted and passed into a later request, which is how the connected flow stays realistic.

Single endpoint tests answer whether one call works, and scenario tests answer whether the ordered, connected flow works, with shared variables and assertions at every step. Both earn a place in a healthy suite: isolated tests give speed and breadth, scenarios catch the broken chains that only appear across calls. Treat them as layers, not substitutes, and remember that a 200 on one request says nothing about the steps that follow. More in the API scenario testing guide.
