#9679. 9 Ways To Upgrade Your Burger King Breakfast Order

All too often we have to settle for a protein bar or a lackluster cup of coffee as a way to start the day. So, when we finally treat ourselves to a breakfast sandwich, pancakes, or some hash browns, they need to be good. Part of making that morning stop worth it is being able to customize the meal just the way you like it. So, if you're making the trip to Burger King for breakfast on the way to work, school, or a day out, here are some ways to up your order's flavor and value in a few quick steps.

And just to make things as easily understood as possible, consider going into the restaurant to order for any multi-step adjustments. It'll cut down on the confusion that can sometimes happen through an app. But however you choose to order, be sure to arrive before the 10:30 a.m. cutoff so you can get the breakfast you've been dreaming of.

Prices can vary from location to location. All pricing information in this article is from a San Diego, California Burger King. Please check the website or app for your local restaurant to confirm current costs.

Hash browns are already a crunchy part of Burger King's breakfast burritos, so why not carry that over to the sandwiches, too? It adds texture, flavor, and keeps you from having to reach into the bag over and over again. It's also a tip that can carry over to other establishments. For instance, you can use the spuds to elevate your next Egg McMuffin (or just about any other breakfast sandwich you'd like). At a San Diego BK location, a side of hash browns costs $3.29, just in case you want to add extra to what comes with a combo meal.

There are several ways to do this flavor hack, with some fans suggesting combining the meat and eggs from a breakfast sandwich on a burger with the tots. Others say to keep it simple and place a few of the crispy potatoes on a Croissan'wich with one, or a few types, of the many sauces available. But, really, however you feel you should be customizing the sandwich in the moment is the right choice.

If you're a fan of soft, sweet pancakes and sausage, bacon, or ham, why not combine them into the ultimate DIY breakfast sandwich? The restaurant's pancake platter makes this one of the easiest hacks overall, but the catch is not every location will have them. However, those getting breakfast in one that does can grab the platter and already have the components they need for an incredibly sweet and savory sausage sandwich. The diner can even decide whether they want to drizzle syrup on the pancakes, dunk them, or both.

It's easy to up the protein for more hearty options, too. If you don't happen to see the option to buy just an extra sausage patty or bacon on the app or in-store menu board, don't worry. A BK employee on Reddit said the restaurant can sell different individual ingredients, as long as the worker knows how to ring it up and what's currently available.

French toast sticks combine the crispiness of hash browns and the sweetness of syrup into an easy way to add both to your sandwich or burger in one move. An order is $3.29 at one San Diego location, so it likely won't put much of a dent in your wallet either. This might appear to be a questionable move, but fans of the convenience store Sheetz's French toast sticks already know using the bread as a way to complement eggs, bacon, cheese, and jalapeños, is a crowd-pleaser.

People praise Burger King's version of the crunchy pieces of toast, including some vegetarians and vegans who note the item is made without dairy or eggs. However, the company notes that the sticks might share equipment with dairy products in case you need to avoid it. For those who do put the toast on their sandwiches, the bread's crispy exterior combining with the other ingredients makes it a uniquely tasty meal you'll be sure to remember.

Want more flavor and a creamy texture added to your breakfast? Mix and match the many Burger King sauces and jams for unexpectedly delicious upgrades to the burritos, burgers, and sandwiches. Condiments like the picante sauce, barbecue sauce, honey mustard, and grape or strawberry jelly can be spread directly onto the item, used as a dip, or mixed together to do both. Many of them don't cost extra, but the ones that do are less than a quarter at a BK location in San Diego.

A Reddit user posted about their order, saying, "Did the mix and match double sausage croissan'wiches, added the strawberry jam to get a little sweet with all this savory!" Others suggest using ranch to compliment the meal, which is a solid idea because it's herby tang can cut through a bit of grease if necessary. But the ever-dependable ketchup remains on stand-by, too. So, let your tastebuds lead you to creating the perfect mix of flavors for your next breakfast outing.

If you like milk tea and/or iced coffee, this hack is an easy way to meet in the middle by making a pseudo-affogato. An affogato is traditionally made by pouring a shot of espresso over gelato to create a beautiful union of extreme temperatures and taste differences. If you're close to a location that offers ice cream, you can add some BK soft serve to your hot or cold coffee for a sweet and creamy start to the day. At one San Diego restaurant, the hot, brewed coffee cost $2.89 per cup, while the iced coffees are priced at $3.39.

In addition to upping the flavor, this upgrade will also give the coffee a silky quality from the cold dairy. It's a quick way to cool down the hot kind and to sweeten the cold variety, thanks to the soft serve already containing cream, sugar, and vanilla. All in all, this is a great way to have something unique without having to wait in line at a specialty coffee house. We'll call that an early morning win.

For those watching their macros, or if you're just craving some extra meat, adding a burger patty to any of the breakfast sandwiches will give you flame-broiled flavor and lots of protein. Many Burger King locations sell all of its hamburgers during breakfast, so there's no shortage of the patties being cooked. But if you want an extra fresh and hot one, asking for the beef to be "fresh off the broiler" will get you a cooked-to-order patty.

To further customize the sandwich (and add even more protein), some customers combine the contents of a Croissan'wich with a burger. To make the process even easier, diners can order the Fully Loaded Croissan'wich, which comes with bacon, sausage, ham, eggs, and American cheese on buttery bread, and add a hamburger patty to the whole thing or sub out one of the other meats for it. The fully loaded croissant option costs $7.19 at a San Diego location, but the price of an extra patty isn't advertised on the restaurant's website.

Eggs might not sound exciting to everyone, but the soft, unctuous items can easily become the star of the meal on a DIY breakfast burger. Putting an egg, or in this case a BK egg patty, on a regular burger adds flavor, texture, and protein while keeping the sandwich from becoming one-ingredient-too-many. That might have something to do with the way the folded item can take on flavor while staying undeniably eggy. That sponge-like ability allows the egg to take on a sauce, cheese, and beef or plant-based burger and bring out the best in all of them.

The chain has tested the idea of a proprietary breakfast burger called the Bacon Cheddar Hash Whopper that included an egg patty and hollandaise aioli. It was only available briefly in select markets, so those who enjoy this hack will have to keep waiting to order it without asking for modifications to a regular burger.

Eggs aren't just unique in their flavor properties, but their ability to change textures depending on how they're cooked is incredible. They can be so soft they're hard to keep on a fork or so tough they can feel hard to chew through. But there's a middle ground where eggs stay light and fluffy while staying strong enough to keep their shape. That area is what makes taking the bread off a breakfast sandwich or burger and using egg patties for a bun possible. Plus, this is a great way to get rid of carbs while adding protein and a silky consistency.

To get those egg patties at the restaurant, you'll have to ask to double the eggs on your sandwich while requesting no bread. Just know the patty will cost a little extra. You can also order a double meat sandwich and ask to swap a sausage with another egg to make it even easier.

While there are plenty of social media food hacks to avoid (anyone else remember the toaster grilled cheese trend?), there are others that are absolutely inspiring. Using hash browns to make breakfast sandwiches is one. And don't forget the pancakes as a bun, either. All you have to do for this hack is cut them into quarters to have sweet and savory treats in a bite-size form.

So, whether diners want to make their own silver-dollar-esqe sandwiches or use French toast or hash browns for crunchy mini-stacker breakfast versions, this upgrade lets customers fully customize their morning meal while playing with their food. Both the French toast sticks and the hash browns cost $3.29 per order at a BK location in San Diego, but you'll have to inquire at the restaurant for pricing on extra eggs, meat, and/or cheese. Whatever combination you decide on, feel free to mix it up even further by grabbing a few different sauces to complete this DIY upgrade.

#9672. Salmon Is 10x More Delicious When You Add A Spoonful Of This Condiment

Salmon tends to be a heavier, rich fish that benefits from bright ingredients that lighten its final flavor profile. That's why a simple Dijon-crusted salmon has so much going for it: It combines the best of hearty seafood and sharp tang with a breadcrumb sprinkle that guarantees deliciousness.

Mustard is the flavorful binder that makes breaded meat less boring, but it works wonders on any type of protein — whether you're using it for your fish or to slow-cook a pork shoulder. But Dijon goes so far beyond the standard yellow condiment you may use for burgers and hot dogs. Made with dark seeds, vinegar, and splashes of white wine, it's a complex blend of sinus-opening heat, slow fermentation, and earthy herbs. Not only does it cut through the fat of even the most high-quality salmon, but all these tastes together also make it a fairly comprehensive flavoring agent, removing the need for complex seasoning blends and cooking styles.

Whether you're working with farmed or wild salmon, Dijon is the best choice. Wild-caught fish have more complexity, thanks to their oceanic diets, and just a light smear of Dijon provides an equally nuanced ingredient to play off its natural tastes. Farm-raised varieties are often fattier, so a heavier application ensures your filets don't end up tasting too rich. Regardless of the type, mustard provides a potent adhesive for any seasonings you do choose to use, giving your delicate protein a delicious crust and caramelizing into a crispy brown topping.

Just because Dijon is plenty tasty in its own right doesn't mean you can't tweak it for specific recipes. Whether you're pairing it with your breadcrumbs or looking to improve your meat directly, treat it like a compound butter and mix in whatever you have lying around for an easy upgrade.

Both salmon and Dijon are perfect candidates to pair with herbs. However, since fish typically doesn't need long cooking times, it's best to stick with fresh, rather than dried, which take longer for the flavor to bloom. Minced dill, basil, or thyme are easy to add to Dijon and complement its winey notes and pungency. Be careful not to use too much, or anything too potent, as it can work with the Dijon to overpower your fish and make it far more difficult to taste. It may help to whisk a bit of oil into the mustard first, so the herbs and spices bloom in the oven, even under the additional weight of breadcrumbs.

Though some consider it a bit taboo, creating a mustard-cheese blended condiment is a truly next-level way to upgrade your filets — plus, in many cases, seafood and cheese belong together. Mild, high-fat, soft varieties like cream cheese, mascarpone, and camembert blend well with Dijon and won't make a too powerful condiment, though a sprinkle of parmesan or pecorino on top can add some valuable earthiness. This creates great flavor, especially if you abstain from breadcrumbs. The more direct heat helps the mustard-cheese combo caramelize into a deliciously decadent shell, and the excess fat pools right off onto the pan.

#9670. 16 pumpkin recipes, from cakes and cookies to bars and bread: We've got a marbled pumpkin cake, chewy pumpkin cookies, and even pumpkin milk bread.

It’s that time of year when pumpkin spice everything starts appearing on store shelves — candles, lip balm, air fresheners, beer, and of course, the ubiquitous PSL (pumpkin spice latte). That means fall is here, and more importantly, that pumpkin should make a grand return to your kitchen! Pull out your canned pumpkin — or better yet, make your own pumpkin purée — and stock your pantry with pumpkin pie spice, because we have the best pumpkin recipes to bake this fall.

This Pumpkin Swirl Cake takes my breath away every time I unmold it from its intricate loaf pan. The anticipation keeps building until I slice into the pound cake-like loaf and reveal the swirled pattern inside, marbled with both vanilla and spiced pumpkin batter. (Don’t fret if you don’t have the specialty loaf pan — this can also be baked in a standard loaf pan and adorned with a simple confectioners’ sugar icing.)

To make this recipe, you'll need: Patch O Pumpkins Loaf Pan and Pure Vanilla Plus

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice and Sparkling Sugar

A cousin of Belgian-style Liège waffles, these Pumpkin Sugar Crunch Waffles have caramelized edges and a pleasant chew that’s reminiscent of brioche. The yeasted batter has pumpkin in it for flavor and color, plus Swedish pearl sugar that melts into pockets of crispy sugar. The best part? The batter rests overnight, so if you prepare it the night ahead, all you have to do the next morning is scoop and cook the batter for hot, crispy waffles in just a few minutes.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Sugar Crunch Waffles

To make this recipe, you'll need: Swedish Pearl Sugar

I used to make the same pumpkin pie recipe for years, and it always left me wanting a little more excitement. Then I found this Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie and never looked back! The generously spiced filling uses nutmeg, ginger, cloves, and Vietnamese cinnamon to create a more flavorful pie than traditional versions. The secret to its silky-smooth texture? Corn syrup, which is an invert sugar and keeps the custard from becoming grainy. Substitute another invert sugar like honey or maple syrup if you like; I use maple syrup.

Get the recipe: Smooth and Spicy Pumpkin Pie

To make this recipe, you'll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon, Ginger, and Nutmeg

Whenever I have these tender, golden scones on hand, I look forward to getting out of bed the next morning because I know they’re waiting for me. They can be easily customized to use a range of mix-ins, depending on what you have in your pantry. My personal preference is a mix of crystallized ginger and Cinnamon Sweet Bits.

Get the recipe: Harvest Pumpkin Scones (or Gluten-Free Pumpkin Scones)

To make this recipe, you'll need: Mini Diced Ginger and Cinnamon Sweet Bits

If you’re looking for a way to make your whole kitchen smell like fall, these one-bowl, easy pumpkin muffins deliver — and fast. They’re ready in under an hour, so you can spend less time measuring, mixing, and cleaning and more time tackling your autumn bucket list.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Standard Muffin Pan

Making banana bread is an almost weekly activity in my house — except during fall, when we pivot to pumpkin bread instead. This is a quick, easy bake that satisfies my craving for something pumpkin-y, and it uses a simple trick to concentrate the pumpkin flavor and ensure the loaf is perfectly textured: The pumpkin purée is reduced on the stovetop to cook off excess moisture. (The process is similar to browning butter.) As a result, the final loaf is packed with pumpkin flavor.

Get the recipe: The Most Pumpkin Pumpkin Chocolate Chip Bread

To make this recipe, you'll need: Ginger and Semisweet Chocolate Chips

These bars have all the cozy, spiced goodness of the classic dessert in a portable, crowd-friendly form. The buttery, brown sugar crust gets pressed into the pan (no rolling out pie dough!), and the silky pumpkin filling comes together with just a handful of ingredients. The (optional but highly recommended) sour cream whipped topping brings a slight tanginess and completes the traditional pumpkin pie experience.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

This Pumpkin Milk Bread is exceptionally soft, squishy, and feather-light, while also packing in a lot of pumpkin. Pumpkin can often weigh down baked goods, but here the combination of a tangzhong, bread flour, and a long mix makes this bread simultaneously moist and high-rising.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant Yeast

This tender pumpkin crumb cake is for people who double the chocolate chips in pumpkin bread and the streusel on coffee cake. Atop the thin layer of spiced pumpkin cake lays a heavy blanket of buttery crumbs with a bold chocolate flavor, thanks to Dutch-processed cocoa powder.

Get the recipe: Chocolate-Pumpkin Crumb Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Black Cocoa

These Pumpkin Cupcakes, with their piped swirl of cream cheese frosting, are the ideal way to celebrate fall birthdays. The cupcakes are super tender, thanks to the addition of cake flour and oil. Sour cream and brown sugar add tanginess and molasses-y sweetness while also preventing the cupcakes from being dry.

For more cupcake decorating ideas, see our YouTube video: Decorate Cupcakes Better Than Ever.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Cake Flour (or Gluten-Free Measure for Measure Flour)

My husband’s favorite fall dessert is Pumpkin Whoopie Pies, hands down. He can’t resist these subtly sweet cakes sandwiching rich cream cheese filling. This recipe has a few extra bells and whistles to take it over the top: Bread and Cake Enhancer to keep the cakes extra soft and fresh, xanthan gum in the filling to give it a smooth mouthfeel, and diced crystallized ginger for a bit of extra zing in the filling.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Bread and Cake Enhancer, Xanthan Gum, and Mini Diced Ginger

The next time there’s a rainy weekend, I’m taking on a project bake: our Pumpkin Cream Cheese Danish. It’s a multiday process and laminating dough is a labor of love, but the final product is worth the effort: buttery, crisp pastries filled with pumpkin and sweet cream cheese.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Cream Cheese Danish

This Pumpkin Layer Cake with Cream Cheese Frosting is a show-stopping dessert featuring spiced layers of cake, not-too-sweet cream cheese frosting, and a blanket of melted caramel poured over the top. Will it be slightly messy to serve? Yes. Will anyone mind? Absolutely not.

The pumpkin spice recipe I’m most excited to bake this fall is a mash-up of greats: Part-coffee cake, part-Bundt cake, part-pumpkin bread, this Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake deserves a category all of its own. It has two layers of espresso swirl tucked within a moist, spiced cake. Make it in your favorite Bundt pan or serve it as a loaf if you’re more of simple-is-better person. Either way, it’s great for snacking all day long.

#9666. 18 Must-Visit Jewish Delis In America

The Jewish deli has been a staple of the American culinary scene since the late 1800s, when immigrants from Europe came to New York and Los Angeles and started serving foods from the old countries. After all, what could be more quintessentially American than a massive corned beef or pastrami sandwich, served on mustard-smeared bread sliced thin enough that it's barely there, and washed down with a salty pickle and a black cherry or Dr. Brown's cream soda?

Some old-school deli orders, like the liverwurst sandwich, you rarely see any more, but many other less familiar staples became widely embraced, though diners in New Jersey had to learn the hard way that a sloppy Joe in a Jewish deli is not going to bring back memories of school cafeterias, and is, instead, a triple-decker cold cut sandwich. With Jewish delis becoming such a cherished institution, there are many to choose from; here are some of the best the country has to offer.

Katz's is the ultimate embodiment of a New York Jewish Deli. The oldest deli in a city known for them, Katz's can trace its legacy back to 1888, and it's still going strong.

This is the place to be if you want to experience what the cultural touchstone is all about, and not just to do your best "When Harry Met Sally" homage. Being a landmark does come with downsides: the food is expensive – the signature pastrami sandwich runs a cool $30.95 — and the lines can be...  intense. That doesn't diminish the quality, or the feeling of history that comes from biting into one of those massive stacks of meat. Try the Katz deli employee menu hack and get a side knish, slice it in half, then pile the meat in between the two sides of the knish. If you are going the traditional route, just make sure to avoid the rookie mistake of ordering white bread for your sandwich.

Ask citizens of Los Angeles what the best Jewish deli in the region is, and you're likely to ignite a debate between two places: Brent's or Langer's (apologies to the other challengers). While younger than some, Brent's is generally considered to be the most well-rounded of the L.A. Jewish delis.

Cheese blintzes served with sour cream and strawberry preserves, stuffed cabbage (which is one of Ukraine's must-try comfort foods), and kasha varnishkas (a dish of bowtie pasta with buckwheat groats) are some popular appetizers before you get to the sandwich options. There's the classic corned beef and brisket, but there are also more adventurous items like hot tongue, chopped liver, and rare roast beef.

If you're trying out Brent's, the natural next step is to also give Langer's a shot, if only in the interest of science. After all, you might as well make a day of it.

If Brent's is the jack-of-all-trades, Langer's is more of a specialist. Sure, it has all the familiar staples, but there's one item that it's known for: the pastrami. Langer's doesn't just make a good pastrami sandwich. It makes one of the best pastrami sandwiches in the country, or, as writer Nora Ephron proclaimed in 2002, possibly the best in the world. The meat is steamed for up to five hours until it can fall apart on your fork, and that time and care make all the difference. The No. 19 — pastrami, Swiss cheese, and coleslaw with Russian dressing — is the go-to here.

If there's any city that you can trust to find the perfect intersection of Jewish culinary tradition and meat sandwiches, it's Chicago, once known as The Slaughterhouse of the World. Manny's Cafeteria and Delicatessen has been in business since 1942, and while the prices might be eye-opening, the food is worth it.

If Langer's is where you go to get top-flight pastrami and Katz's is where you go to have what she's having, then Manny's is where you go to get some of the best corned beef this side of Ireland. Piled ludicrously high atop two thin slices of bread with a slather of spicy horseradish mustard, this is in many ways the perfect sandwich. The recipe has been passed from son to son, and the dedication to the craft shines through in every bite. Potato pancakes, liver and onions, and short ribs are other favorites. It has become a pit stop for politicians such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Barack Obama, and is such a favorite of Obama's former chief of staff, David Axelrod, that it's been described as his second office.

There are plenty of reasons to come to this Ann Arbor destination, but one stands out above the rest: its signature sandwich has a strong claim as one of the best Reuben sandwiches in America. The corned beef is made with love and attention, utilizing freshly squeezed garlic juice used instead of garlic powder for maximum flavor. That attention to detail is what has made it a destination for meat-lovers the world over, resulting in what the restaurant claims is about 50,000 No. 2 Reuben sandwiches made each year.

While most of the delis on this list cling to the traditional ways, the James Beard-nominated Larder Delicatessen and Bakery in Cleveland has a more modern spin. Chef Jeremy Umansky takes global ingredients and techniques and adds them to the rich cultural heritage, resulting in Larder being named one of the best Jewish Delis in America.

Like any other spot on this list, you're going to find pastrami here. But are any of the other delis brining their pastrami for three days in koji, the ultimate meat marinade? Don't worry — the mold spores in koji are safe, and the desire to innovate at Larder doesn't take away from the feeling of comfort that comes when you bite into one of these special sandwiches. Don't neglect the ample selection of pickles, which includes plums, kosher dill carrots, sweet mustard green tomatoes, and rhubarb.

New York is likely the first place that comes to mind when you think of Jewish delis, but you probably don't get too far down the list before you hit New Jersey, and Hobby's Deli in Newark is one of the best the Garden State has to offer. Hobby's has been called a top-10 deli in America by some and has been praised for having the best pastrami in America by others, as it proudly proclaims on its website. It also has the motto "Established before you were born," which, technically, is true.

While the current family owners, the Brummers, have "only" been running it since 1962, there has been a deli in that location since at least 1910. It's such an institution that the street it's on was dubbed Hobby Plaza by the city of Newark in 2014. It also happens to be a favorite of anyone in need of some nourishment before hitting a New Jersey Devils hockey game, as the Prudential Center is a six-minute walk away.

If you're an out-of-towner, you could be forgiven for not knowing that Skokie, Illinois, is the place to go for elite deli food. The town has a vibrant history of Jewish heritage post-World War II, with a Jewish population of around 40,500 people by 1977.

As is the case with Manny's in Chicago, where Jewish neighborhoods and a history of high-quality meat intersect, can't-miss delis are sure to follow. Enter Kaufman's Bagel and Delicatessen, which boasts some of the best sandwiches in the city. The pastrami is good, the matzo ball soup is nourishing, but the star of the show is the New Jersey Bypass sandwich. This two-tiered monstrosity (a word meant as the highest compliment) puts to rest the age-old question of pastrami or corned beef with a dignified solution: Why not have both stacked on top of each other?

When it comes to this topic, I have a simple rule: if you're good enough to last over a century as a Jewish deli on the Upper West Side, you're good enough for me. Barney Greengrass, also known as the Sturgeon King, has been a staple among New York's deli diners since 1908.

The sheer variety of the food offered will blow newcomers away and make it a must-try. You can get smoked meat sandwiches here, but, as the nickname suggests, this is really the spot to be if you're looking for smoked fish. Sturgeon is what the deli is most famous for, but it also has caviar, pickled herring in cream sauce, kippered herring, and smoked salmon so delicious it earned the title of Anthony Bourdain's best breakfast in NYC as well as Andrew Zimmern's second-favorite lox and cream cheese stop in New York City.

We know your New York deli dance card is getting dangerously full, but we have to add just one more option. Over in the Bronx and Westchester sits Liebman's Deli, a neighborhood staple in the former since 1953.

Liebman's might not have the instant name recognition of Katz's, but that's a matter of branding, not quality. It is considered one of the best in the country, with fluffy matzo balls, some of the finest pastrami in New York City, and old-school classics like kreplach (beef-filled dumplings) soup. It also has specialties like hot dogs wrapped in knish dough and tongue polonaise, which features beef tongue simmered in raisin gravy. If there's one thing you have to try, it's the Liebman's Favorite: an open-faced mountain of pastrami and corned beef served with fries and gravy-soaked dermas, a meatless sausage made from matzo meal and animal fat.

Shapiro's sandwiches are not for the faint of heart, but their prestige isn't just predicated on size. These sandwiches are seriously delicious, with recipes honed since 1905. It boasts of being the oldest single-family deli in America, having originally opened its doors in 1905 after the Shapiros emigrated from the USSR, but its roots go even further back than that. According to restaurant lore, the family's predecessors ran a grocery in Odessa, Ukraine, in 1795, giving them the claim of over two centuries of family-run deli experience. Don't neglect the cherry cheesecake, which is considered one of the best in town.

Katzinger's is another Midwest must-try when it comes to the Jewish deli scene. As with many good delis, there's a small but lively grocery inside selling cakes, cheeses, and, naturally, pickles out of a wooden barrel, but let's be real — you're here for the sandwiches.

The Katzinger's Reuben (a corned beef delicacy) is hard to pass up, but the deli also has a similar version with chopped chicken liver added to it, known as Steve's Cross Currents, and the Bill, Gary and Beuford's Upper Yough Reuben (aka the No. 39) was featured on the Food Network's "Best Thing I Ever Ate!"

It's hard to stand out in the Bay Area when it comes to the sandwich game. After all, San Francisco is the city that invented Dutch crunch sandwich bread and helped popularize sourdough bread.

But even with all the competition such innovation spawned, Saul's Restaurant and Delicatessen has managed to distinguish itself as one of the best sandwich spots in the area. While the owners changed in 2022, it has continued on in the tradition that has made it so beloved, serving classics like liver and onions and Reubens along with innovations like a corned beef sandwich with mayonnaise and jalapeno-cilantro zhoug. If you're looking for something in the poultry family, the chicken schnitzel with challah breading and za'atar is a favorite.

Mamaleh's is a relative newcomer on the scene, boasting that it's been "noshing in since 2016." But what it lacks in experience, it makes up for in Yiddish lessons, creative drinks (homemade celery soda or sparkling pickled cucumber lemonade, anyone?), and all the classics.

The baked goods are considered some of the best that the Boston area has to offer, starting with Mamaleh's homemade bagels, challah rolls, and bialys. On the sweet side, the deli has its "soon to be world-famous chocolate cake" and a chocolate babka French toast, among other items And then there's the fish. For $40, you can get the smoked fish platter for two, which comes with whitefish salad, lox, cream cheese, all the fixings, and two homemade bagels.

Confidence is a major part of performance, so when Famous 4th Street Deli advertises itself as "the best deli in America," we want to take the claim seriously. Luckily, it's hard to find too much fault with the claim. After all, if there's one thing Philly knows, it's thinly-sliced beef sandwiches.

This Michelin-recognized deli has been in operation since 1923, slinging sandwiches the size of zeppelins, potato pancakes, and a delicious special matzo ball soup with kreplach, noodles, rice, and kasha. The pastrami and eggs are a must-try for breakfast, but once lunch rolls around, it's time to try the sandwiches, whether the traditional style or the open-faced brisket smothered in gravy. Plus, it wouldn't be a Philadelphia without the restaurant's Famous Cheesesteak, which contains brisket, pastrami, and corned beef.

Attman's Deli has been a mid-Atlantic landmark since 1915. And in that time, it has earned its reputation as one of the best Jewish delis in the country the hard way. Did you know that Baltimore has a stretch of street called Corned Beef Row?

Out of all that history, Attman's has emerged as the king of the corned beef. The Reubens are universally loved, and there's no better place to eat it than in the Kibbitz Room, which is what the restaurant calls its attached dining room. The place also offers more off-the-beaten-path items like hot dogs topped with bologna, Maryland crab soup, and The Gay Liveration, which features corned beef, chopped liver, Swiss cheese, lettuce, and sweet Bermuda onion.

We couldn't help but make one last stop in the Tri-State Area. Harold's Famous Deli, in Edison, New Jersey, is not cheap, but what it lacks in wallet-friendliness, it makes up for in dedication to scale.

The claim to fame is sandwiches meant to be shared. The monster pastrami sandwich serves two to three people and runs for $48.95, while the extra large, which serves four to seven, is $105.95 (individual sandwiches, known as "the junior," are also available starting at $27.95). The matzo ball soup is $35.95 and is recommended for three people. Even the pancakes are meant to be shared, and start at $26.95 for a single flapjack. If you're not scared away by those prices, you're in for a real treat because this isn't a gimmick restaurant. The meat is well-cooked, the kid's menu includes fried clams, and did we mention there's a complimentary pickle bar?

1173 King Georges Post Rd, Edison, NJ 08837

Philadelphia isn't the only Pennsylvania city boasting mean deli eats. Squirrel Hill Market, located in one of Pittsburgh's most prominent Jewish neighborhoods, might not have the same name recognition as some of the other entries here, but it's no less deserving.

This is a smaller establishment than many of the others on the list, with a more limited grocery selection, but when it comes to layering on the corned beef, there is no skimping. The restaurant advertises its sandwiches as containing "one full pound of what you've been missing," alongside other sizable selections such as a footlong pastrami or corned beef dog (yes, there's a hot dog in there somewhere), and even a Reuben bowl.

To create this list, I used a variety of methods to ensure that the scope reached as many corners of the country as possible. Many of the recommendations come from years of personal experience as a dedicated hunter for the perfect smoked meat sandwich, a quest passed along by my father, whose recommendations also helped shape this list. Others were added due to overwhelming consensus among reviews and online commenters.

#9665. Have Yourself A Chrissy Little Christmas

Chrissy Teigen is trading a picture-perfect holiday for homemade ornaments, flour-dusted counters, and a verrry full house.

Christmas for Chrissy Teigen, cookbook author and founder of the food and bakeware brand Cravings by Chrissy Teigen, means getting the whole crew together: her husband, award-winning artist and producer John Legend; their four kids; three dogs; a bearded dragon; and a parrot. There’s a lot going on under one roof.But Chrissy handles chaos with ease. These days, she’s more focused on making memories with Luna, 10, Miles, 8, Esti, 3, and Wren, 3, than on making everything perfect.Much of that joy happens in the kitchen, where Chrissy has built a career writing three best-selling cookbooks and launching a line of baking mixes in unexpected flavors, like snickerdoodle with miso-honey sugar.The family travels often, but Chrissy is looking forward to staying put this winter. It’ll give her more space to embrace the spontaneity she’s craving this year—the kind you can find only when you’re home for the holidays.

Chrissy Teigen: Oh, Halloween. We have a big kids’ Halloween party here at the house. We pick a theme and run with it. This year we picked Coraline.

We love crafting so much. I wanted to stay home for the holidays this year because I need all my children to start hand-making their ornaments and putting them on the tree. I’ve entered this time in my life where I want Christmas to be completely whimsical and over the top. I want to have a cute, colorful, chaotic Christmas this year. I want to thread the popcorn onto the string and have the most chaotic kids’ Christmas tree ever. And I can’t wait for that.

Cooking, of course. Scalloped potatoes in my house are very, very holiday. And my mom comes to town. She lives in Thailand, so we love getting the whole family together. And there’s a lot of football. John’s family loves it, and there’s usually a big Ohio State game around Thanksgiving that they all go crazy for. They go just as nuts for the Christmas game, too. It’s very much the whole family on the floor of my house, watching everything together, and it’s beautiful.

It will be filled with so much joy, but it’s going to be an emotional one for me, of course. To have that big yellow chair that my dad loved so much, empty...I don’t exactly know what to expect from me emotionally, but I can imagine it will be all the things that make the holidays so complex: sad and wonderful and special all at the same time.We will bake, with love, the potatoes Dad loved so, so much. We will clean the greens the way Granny (on John’s side) told us to. I’m sure our eyes will well up. It’ll be a testament to how much they meant to us all.

It is, but that recipe has always haunted me. My mom is impossible to get a recipe from. I think a lot of moms do this on purpose: You ask them to share a recipe, and something’s missing, or they leave out one little thing.I’ve checked in about this one so many times. She’s made it twice a year my whole life, and every time I ask about a detail—whether she uses MSG or when she adds the pepper—I get a different answer. So I’m not even sure I have the right recipe in my cookbook. Whenever she makes it, something is different. You could call it a mom’s touch, but I think she’s leaving out an important ingredient because she wants hers to be the best.

We do Tyler Florence’s beef Wellington every year. It looks impressive, but it’s quite simple, and it’s never gone wrong for me. When I cut into it, the color is beautiful, and it’s juicy. Over the years, I’ve learned how to keep the pastry crisp, even on the bottom where the meat juices collect. It’s a flawless recipe, and the peppercorn sauce is amazing. It pleases everyone, and the kids can cut shapes out of the puff pastry. For sides, we have the scalloped potatoes, green beans, and carrots.

My girls are always in the kitchen with me—I’m not allowed to cook without them. I love it, even though it slows things down. Esti is kind of the boss of the house right now, and she gets nervous that if she goes upstairs to shower, we’ll finish the recipe without her. We make sure she’s back in time to cook the recipe from beginning to end. I expect Esti and Luna will do most of the cooking for Christmas dinner.

No, they’re more likely to spill things. The living room is always covered in spills. I often put my drink on the floor because the table is too far away, and the boys knock it over with their feet.

Miles is our “won’t eat anything” guy. He’s eight now, and he’s been picky since he started eating solid food. He mostly likes chicken nuggets, fries, hamburgers, and pizza. Esti’s tastes change quickly. She might want apples with every dinner, then decide she doesn’t like them—and be like, “I never liked apples. Are you crazy?”Wren is our tank. He’ll eat anything. He gets almost catatonic when he’s eating, so he forgets it could make him sick.Luna knows how to make foods taste better. If something has a burnt corner, for example, she’ll cut it off or find another way to improve it. I think that’s really special.

I remember not liking raw tomatoes or avocados when I was young, even though I love them now, so I’m not too worried about how the kids’ tastes will change. They’re kids, and they’re told what to do all day. Food can be one way they speak up and feel like their opinions matter. I get that—it must be hard to be told what to do from morning to night. As long as they’re full and not waking up hungry, I’m fine.

Christmas morning is an all-day experience for us. Once my kids open a present, they want to play with it, so they take their time instead of rushing through the gifts. I used to have so many rules and run around stressing about the wrapping and recycling. Now I just relax and let the day unfold.

I love prepping for Christmas the night before, especially when it’s a secret, and I’m in charge. I’ll make hot cocoa bombs. In the morning, the kids just have to pour hot milk over them. And we’ll have pancakes, bacon, and Mrs. Butterworth’s syrup, get a sugar rush, and then hopefully have like a nice midday crash together.

Luna has always wanted to be in on the secret. I worried that, as my oldest, she might feel like she was missing out on the Christmas magic, but she loves helping make it special for her younger siblings. Last year, I asked if she wanted to stay up all night with me, and she loved that more than anything.She and Esti also love making stockings for the dogs, the bearded dragon, and now the parrot. We had lots of animals growing up, and I remember my mom taking me to PetSmart to pick out little gifts for our bird. I made sure every beating heart in the house got celebrated, and now the kids love doing that, too.

The bearded dragon toy industry is small. Last year we got little inflatable pools, and there are dried insects, as gross as they are. And a little Santa hat. He’s happy with that. I used to make bird toys with my dad for our parrot, so getting things for Audrey reminds me of that time with him.

Without a doubt, and I’m putting Luna in charge. Carrot cake is our family’s favorite. It was my wedding cake, and it’s John’s family’s favorite, too. There’s so much warmth in it: It has spices and real carrots, and it’s sticky, decadent, and delicious. It’s our holiday pleaser.In addition to our carrot cake kit, I hope we can one day offer a kit with lots of elements for people to decorate a cake and have fun with. The holidays are all about slowing down and getting your hands into something, and it doesn’t hurt if you can eat it after, too.

No, but I loved baking mixes, especially confetti cake mix. My dad had a big sweet tooth, and baking mixes and TV dinners were important to me. My mom’s food seemed too spicy or daunting when I was a kid, so my dad and I bonded over Hungry-Man dinners, Kid Cuisine, and Hot Pockets. Homemade food was mostly for the holidays.I think that’s why grocery stores still excite me. I take my kids shopping and love seeing what’s new—and finding foods that taste just like I remember, like frozen Salisbury steak. Those were the foods I grew up on, and I wanted to recreate them at home for my Cravings cookbooks. I’ve never looked down on those foods. They’ve stood the test of time for a reason. They’re nostalgic and wonderful.

#9664. What are flour enzymes?: Understanding a common flour ingredient.

If you look closely at a bag of King Arthur flour, you may see an unfamiliar ingredient listed there: enzyme.

We’re extremely thoughtful about every ingredient we use, across all King Arthur products and recipes. Our Food Philosophy guides every decision to ensure the quality of what we create, and that includes the enzymes in our flour.

Here’s exactly what flour enzymes are and why they’re included in flour.

Enzymes are found naturally in wheat, and thus are already present in flour. An enzyme is a protein produced by a living organism that acts as a catalyst to bring about a specific biochemical reaction.

The amount of enzymes in flour can vary based on growing conditions from harvest to harvest and year to year, so we add natural enzymes to correct for any variance and make sure our flour bakes more consistently — in other words, to make your baking even better. Those enzymes make up a very small portion of the total flour: less than 1%.

The enzyme we use in our flour is technically called fungal alpha-amylase. That’s a pretty technical name, so it is commonly labeled simply as “enzyme” on ingredient labels. “Alpha-amylase” is the actual enzyme, and “fungal” refers to the fact that the living organism that produces the enzyme is a fungus, not unlike yeast or a mushroom. Amylase may sound unfamiliar, but your body makes and uses it every day. When you eat, it begins breaking starch into smaller carbohydrates so you can draw on it for energy. Amylases added to flour perform a similar function.

Note: Though fungi are technically living organisms, enzymes are considered vegan, as they are not animal based.

Malted barley is an alternative source of enzymes that King Arthur has used in the past, but we found the efficacy can vary batch to batch. By swapping malted barley for straight enzymes, the flour produces more consistent results for our bakers.

Another reason we made the switch? Enzymes require less water and energy to produce than malt barley. As a Certified B Corporation, we're committed to being good stewards of our planet, so pivoting to a responsibly sourced ingredient with a smaller environmental footprint makes sense.

To put it simply, enzymes are added to flours to improve baking performance — they do not change the flour's nutritional value. More specifically, they help create the foods that feeds yeasts. The enzymes break down complex starches into simpler sugars; this, in turn, provides yeast with readily available fermentable sugar (food!), which enables yeast to work continuously and supports both fermentation and crust browning. This results in improved bread volume and crumb texture. Most other manufacturers of flour and yeasted mixes use enzymes for the very same reasons.

Ultimately, enzymes are yet another way for us to provide you with the most consistent flour — which means even better baking.

#9660. Skip Ground Chuck: The Ideal Type Of Ground Beef For Tacos With Big Flavor

It goes without saying that meat forms the cornerstone of a ground beef taco. Yet while so many cooks focus on adding something (like cocoa powder) to ground beef for richer tacos, fewer pay attention to the cut at hand. After all, minced meat takes on not only various fat compositions, but can originate from different parts of the animal, each of which translates into a unique flavor and texture.

Especially common on grocery shelves is a product simply labeled ground beef, which means the meat mix consists of bits and pieces sourced from all around the cow. Also popular is ground chuck, a cut that turns out rich when ground, perfect for burgers and meatballs that will hold their shape during cooking. For tacos, though, reach for ground round instead; it's the ideal type for a flavorful pan-fried filling.

Round comes from a broad region near the back legs of a cow. It's an area high in connective tissue, but leaner than chuck. As a result, the ground beef doesn't turn too greasy when cooked, instead producing lean bites of meat that are amenable to the dish. The flavor is milder, too — making it an ideal canvas for your chosen seasonings. Put together, such characteristics yield a tasty beef character, but one that won't overwhelm your taco build.

Making the best ground beef taco meat is different from other recipes. Fat is flavor, and with the round's leaner composition than chuck, you're getting a less beefy experience. If you're looking to make juicy burger patties, that's a detractor. For ground beef tacos, though, such a restrained character is beneficial.

Aim for a ground round composition of around 85% lean and 15% fat beef. There's still enough fat to keep bites tender, but not an excess that'll have oil pooling in the pan. You'll let the intricate flavor of taco seasonings shine, but the beef still comes with its own delicate nuance. You can get unorthodox and add some of the best seasonings for beef, like pairing Guajillo chile powder with honey.

Furthermore, the ground round bits will cook down into a crumble, which lets you adhere spice onto a greater surface area. And once rolled into a tortilla or crispy taco shell, the beef is loose in tiny pieces, as is classic with the dish. Ground round strikes a perfect balance, making a taco rendition that hits the right notes without overwhelming the dish.

#9656. Costco Customers Order The Chocolate Cake With This One Adjustment For A Massive Flavor Boost

"Like a gigantic, delicious Hostess Suzy Q," one commenter on a Reddit thread devoted to this swap said (we can almost hear their mouth watering through the internet). Another Costco customer wrote that the employee at their bakery suggested they do this for their daughter's birthday cake, and the results were so, so good. "Rave reviews from the party guests," they declared.

If you can find a Costco bakery to pull off this feat of cake deliciousness (more on that later), it stands to reason you could also request the inverse. If you're not a huge fan of chocolate cake (or you're serving those that aren't), but you do enjoy chocolate mousse filling, you have options!

It seems that you used to be able to order this opposite-flavor combination cake on the actual order form at the Costco bakery, but that is no longer the case. In fact, you might not be able to get a chocolate cake with vanilla cheesecake mousse filling (or vice versa) at all if your bakery doesn't allow for this customization, which some very likely might not. So how can you be sure? While there are no direct phone lines to the individual bakeries, you could try calling the store and requesting that someone ask the bakery on your behalf.

If you have received a response in the affirmative (or perhaps, you know others who have already obtained cakes like these from your location), it's also in your best interest to place the order at least a week ahead of when you'll need it, to give the bakery plenty of time to make the necessary adjustments. If you're making the cake arrangements the old-fashioned, and frankly outdated, way in-store on the form, where it reads, "Filled with 2 lbs. X mousse," you can just cross out the flavor of mousse you don't want, and write in the flavor you do want.

If you're taking advantage of Costco's new cake ordering upgrade on its app, however, you might instead include a message about the desired swap in the Notes section at the end of the form. It's just important to remember that whichever way you choose, it's of tantamount importance that you include your phone number, so the bakery can reach out to confirm details if needed.

#9654. 7 Costco Foods You Should Buy Early For Thanksgiving—And 5 You Should Skip

Visit the warehouse before it becomes a madhouse.

It’s November, so it’s officially time to plan and shop for your Thanksgiving menu. And if you’re planning to feed a crowd and would prefer to stay within budget, it’s no surprise that Costco is one of the best places to stock up on ingredients. That is, if they’re even in stock.

The warehouse is more like a madhouse in the days leading up to major holidays. Shopping early allows you to check everything off your list and spares you a lot of stress later this month. However, not all ingredients are worth buying in advance.

I write about food and Costco for a living, and as much as I love the bulk warehouse, I can still be honest about what you shouldn’t buy. Here are the warehouse essentials I’d recommend buying early for your Thanksgiving dinner—and the things I’d skip.

Williams Sonoma suggests serving anywhere from half to an entire bottle of wine per guest at Thanksgiving. And if your local Costco sells booze, the warehouse often carries solid-quality bottles at a fraction of the retail price.

From gravy to stuffing, chicken stock serves as the foundation of some essential holiday foods. Kirkland Signature’s shelf-stable cartons are a great thing to buy ahead of time so you’re ready to go on Thanksgiving.

If you want to avoid washing your fine china and pressing linen napkins, disposable plates, silverware, and napkins are key. Costco is currently offering a wide range of options. Whether you want festive, fall-themed paper plates or elegant heavyweight plastic ones, you can save a lot of money on your tablescape by using Costco serving supplies.

If you’re baking desserts from scratch this year, Costco is the ideal spot to stock up on ingredients. From vanilla extract to pecans to cans of pumpkin puree, the warehouse carries everything you need in sizes large enough to feed your whole extended family.

Whether you’re serving them mashed, scalloped, or marshmallow-topped, you’ll most likely serve some sort of potato at your Thanksgiving feast. A 10-pound bag is one of those no-brainer Costco purchases that you can buy well before the holiday. Just keep the spuds in a cool, dark area until Thanksgiving.

If you’re starting Thanksgiving shopping early, some dairy products won’t last until the big day. Hard cheese is an exception. Costco sells huge blocks of cheddar and Parmesan that can stay unopened and fresh in the fridge for weeks. By the time Turkey Day rolls around, it’ll all be ready to go for homemade mac and cheese, scalloped potatoes, and appetizer spreads.

Butter belongs in virtually every dish on a traditional Thanksgiving menu. And these days, it’s not cheap at standard supermarkets. Thankfully, you can buy it in bulk at Costco. Kirkland Signature’s butter is just as good as brand-name, and it lasts for weeks unopened in the fridge.

Potatoes are sturdy and durable enough to sit in your pantry for weeks, but that doesn't apply to most other vegetables. Leafy greens, herbs, and pre-trimmed green beans will get nasty fast. I’d recommend skipping them on your initial trip and going back closer to the holiday to grab your vegetables.

When you’re shopping ahead of time, I’d recommend steering clear of most baked goods—especially bread—unless you plan to freeze them. Both dinner rolls and full-sized loaves will go stale before Thanksgiving. And, contrary to popular belief, you actually shouldn’t use stale bread in stuffing.

It should go without saying. If you buy milk for Thanksgiving recipes weeks ahead of time, it’ll end up more sour than unsweetened cranberry sauce.

I have mixed feelings about Costco’s pumpkin pie in general, specifically with the no-butter crust. That said, it also doesn’t hold up well if you buy it at least a week in advance. The custardy filling tends to leach moisture and give you the dreaded soggy bottom. If you insist on serving a Costco dessert this year, go for the pumpkin cheesecake instead and freeze it until Turkey Day.

This point comes with some caveats. Costco turkeys are undoubtedly a good deal, but buying them early is not always practical for some households. If you’re buying it ahead of time, the turkey should definitely be frozen to prevent spoilage. But unless you have plenty of freezer space (or a separate chest freezer), I wouldn’t recommend buying a turkey that far in advance.

#9653. Skip The Oil And Eggs: Add A Can Of Diet Coke To This Cake Mix For The Easiest Dessert

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Boxed cake mix is hard to beat when you need a dessert in a hurry, or if you just don't back your baking abilities. One of our favorites is Duncan Hines Devil's Food Cake, available on Amazon, which came in second in our boxed cake mix ranking. Like most packaged options, it comes with all the dry ingredients pre-measured, leaving you to add water, eggs, and vegetable oil. However, just because the instructions are printed on the back doesn't mean you have to follow them to the letter. In fact, you can swap all three for a can of Diet Coke and still come out with a soft, fluffy cake.

To understand why this works, it helps to know what eggs and oil actually do. Egg whites provide proteins that coagulate as the cake bakes, forming a structure that holds the batter together and helps trap the air responsible for its fluffy crumb. The fat from oil and egg yolks coats the flour particles and inhibits gluten development, helping produce a softer, more tender texture. Diet Coke also contributes to the cake's crumb and tenderness, but in a very different way.

Diet Coke's secret weapon is its carbonation. It contains dissolved carbon dioxide, which forms tiny bubbles when added to the batter. As the cake heats up in the oven, these bubbles expand and help the mixture rise. The soda's acidity can also react with leavening agents present in the mix, such as baking soda, further contributing to the cake's light texture. To top things off, a standard 12-ounce can of Diet Coke contains roughly the same volume as the combined water and oil that Duncan Hines' mix calls for, making it a super convenient add-in. If you don't have Diet Coke on hand, Coke Zero is a near-identical substitute.

To get the most out of this swap, start with a can of cold Diet Coke over one that's been sitting at room temperature. Ever noticed how a can of cold Diet Coke has that unbeatable crispness? That's because carbon dioxide prefers to hang around in cold liquids over warm ones. Once a soda can is cracked open, it releases gas, so a cold one retains its carbonation better as you prepare your batter. On that note, avoid over-mixing the batter as this can knock out the trapped gas. If you notice bubbling, that's a telling sign you need to slow down.

When swapping oil and eggs for Diet Coke, there's one important difference worth noting. Diet Coke famously contains no fat, so while it can help the cake rise, it can't replicate the richness that oil brings to the table. It's a great substitution if you're looking to make a lighter, less calorie-dense cake. But for something that'll produce a richer cake with all the same effects as Diet Coke, reach for good old full-sugar Coke instead.

Diet Coke gets its sweetness from aspartame, an artificial sweetener, which loses its sweetness when exposed to heat. Regular Coke opts for high-fructose corn syrup, which is essentially liquid sugar. Unlike aspartame, high fructose corn syrup thrives under heat, and is already a baking superstar. In the oven, its resident sugars caramelize to give the cake a richer flavor, gooier texture, and a beautifully browned color. In fact, any soda will work wonders for boxed cake mix; for a similarly rich flavor profile with a cherry backbone, pick up a can of Cherry Coke or Dr Pepper, or for something brighter, go for Sprite or 7UP.

#9650. Heavy cream vs. whipping cream: What's the difference?: Understanding the right cream for your baking.

If you’re baking a recipe that calls for heavy cream, or picking up a carton to turn into whipped cream to finish a dessert, you may be confused when you hit the dairy aisle. There’s “heavy cream” — but also “heavy whipping cream” or, in some cases, just “whipping cream.”

So when it comes to heavy cream versus whipping cream, is there truly a difference?

Aside from being delicious, there are very specific definitions and standards that must be met in order for something to be labeled as heavy cream. It is made by separating the fatty top layer from the base milk layer during processing. The FDA states that heavy cream is cream that contains no less than 36% milk fat.  Comparatively, milk has 0% to around 3% milk fat, as well as a higher water concentration. Because of its fat content, heavy cream retains a rich taste and, when whipped, it excels at creating stiff peaks that hold their shape for a long time.

Whipping cream — sometimes called “heavy whipping cream” — is made using a similar process as heavy cream and is also the milk fat removed before milk is homogenized. However, whipping cream can contain somewhere between 30% and 35% milk fat content, according to FDA regulations. Because of its slightly lower fat content, it whips into a softer, more billowy cream, and it will deflate more quickly than whipped cream made with heavy cream.

Luckily, the difference in taste and performance between the two types of cream are not very discernible. This means you can use them interchangeably in recipes — and it's okay if you accidentally buy the "wrong" one. Both can yield a delicious bowl of homemade whipped cream. (Can’t justify buying a whole carton of either one? We’ve got you covered with an easy homemade heavy cream substitute.)

A note on King Arthur recipes: The King Arthur Test Kitchen prefers heavy cream in most instances, particularly when making whipped cream, because of the higher fat content. That said, you can substitute heavy whipping cream 1:1 in any King Arthur recipe that calls specifically for heavy cream without any issue.

As a general rule of thumb, use heavy cream for making stable whipped cream for topping pies, layered desserts like tiramisu or banana pudding, and any sweet where the structural integrity hinges on the cream really holding its shape. Heavy cream can also be handy for making cream scones and drop biscuits, where the richness of the dairy can shine through. Stanley Tucci has spent years taking audiences on culinary adventures through Italy, so it’s no surprise S.Pellegrino would tap the icon for a holiday collaboration built around the dinner table. Cocktails aside, one thing he thinks his fans would be surprised to learn is that the devout coffee drinker sometimes enjoys a cup of rooibos tea. “I find it very comforting, particularly when you’re on set, making a movie. That, with a little bit of honey,” he says of how he enjoys the drink.

His actual holiday traditions can get a little more animated. “Around the holidays, sometimes we’ll play charades with the kids in the evening, and it’s just fun because I don’t like to keep score,” he shares. “The fun part of it is watching people get up and trying to get a point across; it’s hysterical to me.”

It’s the generational divide, though, that really makes him laugh.

So while the new S.Pellegrino bottles may get people talking, it’s what unfolds afterward that seems to stick with Tucci most.

His favorite holiday moments are the ones “when people just suddenly start bursting into song, or say, ‘Hey, let’s play charades,’ and then the charades go on forever, all the rules go out the window, and nobody really keeps track of who’s winning or losing,” he says. “That’s the most fun.”

#9642. Forget Mayo: Give Tuna Salad A Major Flavor Boost With This Bottled Ingredient

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

If you're a fan of canned tuna and you get the right stuff, it can be perfectly tasty on a bed of lettuce — it's even one of the best foods to eat straight out of the can. It's a super high-protein food, and when you need a bit more flavor, a tuna salad is one of those simple meals that you can make quickly with just a little good mayo (our favorite being Kewpie) and mustard, maybe some pickle relish or diced cucumbers. That said, there are plenty of easy ways to take your plain tuna salad to the next level, but this is one you may have never thought of. You can skip the mayo completely and use a bottle of store-bought Caesar salad dressing in your next tuna salad. Our top pick for best Caesar salad dressing? Briannas Home Style Asiago Caesar Dressing, available at retailers like Walmart.

Using Caesar dressing in your tuna salad will highlight the salty, umami notes and give some nice vinegary undertones. Even bottled dressings typically have aged Italian cheeses, so they'll add amazing flavor that you can't get from most other off-the-shelf dressings. Plus, even though mayonnaise is often considered a tuna salad's best friend, when the salad is overly mixed (or even whipped with mayo), it can just turn out pasty and gooey and lose the texture of a perfectly good canned tuna altogether. With just a bit of Caesar dressing, mixed simply with a fork, you'll have a beautifully flavored tuna that's ready to add atop a bowl of greens or turn into a sandwich or a proper tuna melt.

Certainly not all Caesar dressings are created equal. Some may be a bit creamier or heavier on the garlic; some may contain anchovies, and some not. If you want more umami, go with something that has anchovies. And if you want the creamy factor that's closer to a traditional homemade tuna salad with mayo, you can often simply check for egg yolks or egg yolk powder on the ingredient list to get that extra hit of smooth, eggy flavor.

For the simplest Caesar tuna salad, per can of regular-sized tuna — which generally runs about five ounces (including the liquid) — you'll want about two and a half tablespoons of Caesar dressing. Whether you go with tuna in oil or in water is purely a personal choice. In oil, of course, the tuna will have more fat, so you may want to use less dressing. To add some crunch, diced onions, cukes, and celery are always a good idea, especially on a sandwich with a little cheese, lettuce, and tomato. Of course, you can add fresh or dried herbs and spices, like smoked paprika or even cayenne powder and hot sauce to add a little more intensity.

If you're making it to add to a full Caesar salad, you can simply toss canned tuna with some romaine lettuce, croutons, and Caesar dressing, then top with a little grated parmesan cheese. Caesar dressing also works great on baked salmon to keep it nice and moist. But when you're making your next simple tuna salad, you can maybe just go with a can of tuna and a few tablespoons of Caesar from the bottle, and you're good to go.

#9641. How to clean cast iron  : It’s simpler than you think.

Despite what you may have heard, cleaning and maintaining a cast iron skillet or Dutch oven isn’t difficult. It’s practically impossible to ruin a well-seasoned skillet, and despite your best efforts, sometimes food will stick. If your cast iron is covered in stuck-on bits of cheese from a batch of Crispy Cheesy Pan Pizza, here's how to clean it.

We can settle the debate once and for all: Yes, you can use soap to clean your cast iron. Dishwashing soap will not damage the seasoning that makes your skillet non-stick. Polymerized oil creates the layer of seasoning through heat, and dish soap isn’t strong enough to break that bond.

No, you cannot clean a cast iron skillet in the dishwasher. This will degrade the seasoning layer and cause it to rust.

You should not soak a cast iron pan either; the water will cause it to rust. If you do end up rusting your pan, you can still rescue it by scrubbing off the rust then re-seasoning the pan.

Using warm, soapy water, scrub the pan with a stiff-bristled brush or sponge to remove any food residue. Avoid harsh, abrasive scrubbers like steel wool or metal pads, which can strip the pan of its seasoning.

Once cleaned, fully dry the pan with a kitchen towel, or place it onto a burner over low heat so the water fully evaporates. Don’t walk away from the pan — it can quickly get smoky once the water has evaporated.

Regardless of which method you prefer, it’s imperative that the pan is fully dry. Water (not soap!) is the enemy of cast iron, which can cause it to rust. Once dry, add a few drops of neutral oil and spread all over the pan with a towel.

#9637. How to proof bread in the oven: Common challenge, simple solution.

During proofing, bread and other yeasted doughs do best in a temperature-controlled, humid, draft-free environment. Your kitchen counter may not cut it (especially in colder months), but is there a corner of your kitchen that fits that description? Yes, your oven — and you don’t even need to fire it up!

Yeast dough is happiest when rising at temperatures between 75°F and 78°F. It will certainly rise in cooler or warmer temperatures. But for most doughs, that range is optimum for both yeast development and bread flavor.

Your oven’s interior will pretty much mirror room temperature. And depending on the time of year (or how much you use air conditioning), that temperature could be pretty cool—too cool for yeast’s comfort.

To get the oven up to that ideal proofing temperature, people often turn to a couple of different methods. I decided to try a bunch of them to see which is best — and helpfully, there was a clear winner.

It’s tempting to simply preheat the oven for a minute or so to warm its interior; but not only is this hit-and-miss (How long should I leave it on? Will the oven get too hot?), it’s ineffective; the heat quickly dissipates once you turn the oven off.

Enter your oven light. When turned on, your oven light’s slow, gentle heat will gradually warm the oven to the desired temperature. After trying a number of different methods for proofing bread in the oven, including several listed below, this was my clear favorite because it created the ideal temperature (not too hot, not too cold), maintained that temperature for several hours, and was essentially failproof (no overshooting the temp, for example!).

It can take your oven a while to reach the desired temperature, especially if your kitchen is cold to begin with. With so many variables — season, climate, kitchen, oven — you’ll want to do a simple experiment to determine your own best method for turning your oven into an effective, efficient proof box:

Take your oven’s temperature before turning on the light. Then turn on the light and measure the temperature again at 15-minute intervals, to see just how quickly the light warms things up. For reference, the light in my electric oven takes about an hour to raise the oven’s interior temperature by 10 degrees, and another hour to raise it an additional five degrees; your results will probably vary a bit.

Warm your oven to about 80°F before turning off the light. Over the next couple of hours, the temperature will gradually drift down by about 10 degrees, giving your rising dough plenty of time in and around that 75°F to 78°F sweet spot.

Once you know how to warm your oven using only its lightbulb, think about maintaining humidity: Dry dough can develop a tough skin, which inhibits rising.

If you’re proofing dough in a bowl (or later, a shaped loaf in a pan), cover it with a clear plastic shower cap or reusable plastic bowl cover. Whatever you use, make sure it's large enough to form a “poof” on top, so the cover doesn’t touch the rising dough.

For shaped rolls (or anything else in a large, flat pan), use an extra-large shower cap; or simply drape the pan with well-greased plastic wrap, waxed paper, or parchment.

What if your oven doesn’t have a light, the lightbulb only lights when you open the oven door, or it’s a “cool” LED bulb?

Then your best bet is a pan of boiling water set on the lowest rack, which will both warm and humidify your oven’s interior. Place the bread dough on the oven’s middle rack; no need to cover it.  Set a shallow pan (e.g., 9" x 13" pan) on the lower rack, and add four cups of boiling water. Quickly close the oven door.

Your oven’s temperature will immediately rise by about 30 degrees, which will probably be warmer than you want. Cool it down by opening the door wide for about five minutes; the temperature should drop about 15 degrees.

As the water in the oven cools, the air around it cools, too. But it happens so gradually that your oven should still remain sufficiently warm for the one to two hours your bread typically needs to rise. For longer-rising breads, simply switch out the cool water with another pan of hot water, if necessary.

Some ovens actually have a proof setting or proofing drawer. I don’t always love using this setting, though: Most are programmed to temperatures ranging from 90°F to 100°F, far warmer than yeast dough’s optimal 75°F to 78°F. For best results, figure out how long it takes to reach about 80°F, then turn it off.

Tip #1: If you have to open the oven door to check your rising dough, don’t worry. Unlike the huge 15- to 20-degree drop you experience when opening a fully heated oven, the temperature inside your light- or steam-warmed oven will only drop by a degree or two.

Tip #2: Typically, you don’t preheat your oven with rising dough inside. So when your dough is close to fully risen, remove it from the oven and set it somewhere safe. (If there’s room, the top of your fridge is both warm and out of harm’s way.) Timed just right, your bread will be perfectly proved by the time the oven finishes preheating.

Tip #3: To prevent someone from killing your rising dough by turning on the oven (say, to warm their leftover pizza), write “NO!” on a sticky note and affix it to the oven’s start button. Really!

For the highly passionate bread baker (or a small baking business), an electronic proof box like the Brod & Taylor Proofer Pro is a step up from proofing dough in the oven. It controls temperature with exquisite precision, from cold-proofing (down to 41°F) for those overnight ferments up to 122°F for an express warmup, all while ensuring perfect humidity. Wi-Fi and programmable timers let you control your dough’s development for up to eight days. It’s literally set it and forget it — the process is simple, but the results are simply amazing.

Still looking for a warm, draft-free spot for your rising bread dough? Think beyond your oven to other major appliances: Both your clothes dryer and dishwasher can double as a proof box!

#9635. Add This Spicy Ingredient To Ground Beef For A Burger That's 10x Juicier

If you're looking for a burger patty that not only has a bit of kick, but also plenty of juice, you need 'nduja, a legendary Italian sausage. It is not only extremely flavorful, but also quite high in fat and moisture, making it a perfect addition no matter how you like to cook your burgers.

'Nduja is technically a type of salami, except it's far more decadent and incorporates a hefty dose of Calabrian chili peppers for next-level taste. Its high fat-to-lean meat ratio makes it perfect for introducing more moisture, even in small amounts. Even if you only have exceptionally lean meat on hand, one part 'nduja to four parts beef keeps your patties tender and juicy, and even helps develop a better crust.

The idea is similar to many meatball recipes from around the world that incorporate both pork and beef. Whereas beef provides body and a hearty texture, pork can provide extra fat, flavor, and moisture, working together to cook up something truly delicious. The peppers also create a slightly savory and spicy flavor profile that, while immediately noticeable, isn't so overwhelming that you might need to change up your preferred toppings. Each bite will drip with flavorful juices that mix with your condiments for the most moisture-rich burger possible.

Incorporating anything into a burger is a bit of a tightrope walk. You want to disperse your ingredients evenly but not work the muscle fibers so much that your patties end up dense or tough. 'Nduja's texture makes this quite easy, but you'll want to be careful about what type of meat you add it to.

Since it has a spreadable, pâté-like texture, working 'nduja directly into the meat is quite easy. Whether you mix it in thoroughly or squeeze pinches into already formed patties for pockets of flavor, you get plenty of fatty juices. Still, if you're worried about overworking your patties or want to add the salty meat at the very last minute, 'nduja is typically safe to eat right out of the package. Treat it like cheese and add a dollop after flipping your patties, letting it melt over the whole thing for a juicy entree.

If you want a custom burger blend, you have to be mindful of the proper fat-to-meat ratio. 'Nduja's exceptional fat content means it's best to add it to already lean blends so you don't end up with anything too greasy. The leaner your beef, the more 'nduja you can incorporate, so it's a balance between how much of its flavor you want included. Something that's at least 85% lean is ideal, letting you incorporate enough to taste without adding so much that you can't appreciate the beef's natural flavor.

#9634. Harvest Caesar Salad

Caesar salad is a year-round favorite in my kitchen, but this harvest spin is on repeat during the fall. Butternut squash pieces are baked with crispy baked Parmesan frico, turning them into cheesy squash “croutons” that give this classic salad the perfect autumnal spin. Trust me—it’s the Friendsgiving dish that everyone will be requesting next year.

The kale:Raw kale can be aggressive, with a rough, almost squeaky texture, so it’s important to treat it by massaging it with both lemon juice and salt before tossing with the dressing. The combination of acid and salt (and your elbow grease!) works together to partially break down the kale fibers, tenderizing it. Wondering how you go about “massaging” the kale? It’s not a science: You literally pretend the bowl of greens is someone’s shoulders. Put your hands in there and massage away!

The croutons:Similar to my crispy Parmesan potatoes, these frico squash croutons are made by roasting the squash on a bed of shredded Parm. In the oven, the cheese melts and caramelizes on the baking sheet, forming this crunchy, crispy crust underneath the squash. This isn’t a difficult technique, but there are a few tips that will make the process much easier.

Make ahead:The frico squash croutons are best fresh (once refrigerated, they’ll lose their crispness), but the dressing can be made 1 day ahead. The kale can also be destemmed and torn up to 1 day ahead, but wait to massage it with the lemon juice and salt until just before serving.
